text:
WASHINGTON -- A federal judge in New York has vacated a Trump administration policy that suspended the processing of visas from 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia, whose nationals the Trump administration deemed likely to require public assistance in the United States.

U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, set aside the policy Friday as "contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority by issuing the policy, which "runs afoul" of the Immigration and Nationality Act by mandating "the refusal of visas to eligible applicants without any basis in law," the judge ruled.

Judge says power lies with consular officers

Vargas said the policy also undermines the congressional requirement that puts consular officers at the forefront of any visa decision.

"Congress imbued these officers with exclusive authority and discretion to determine if an immigrant is eligible for a visa based upon review of specific and detailed criteria set forth in the statute," she wrote. "The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme."

The policy was challenged by two nonprofit organizations along with 11 individuals, including six whose family members had been refused visas. The remaining five are outside the country and had filed "employment-based petitions" to come to the United States.

Advocates say keeping families apart is cruel

"We welcome this ruling because, at its heart, this case is about keeping families together," said Anna Gallagher, the executive director of CLINIC, a national nonprofit that provides training, resources, and support to a network of immigration legal service providers and was one of the plaintiffs.

"Catholic social teaching calls us to uphold the dignity of every person and recognize the family as the foundation of society," she said in a statement. "This decision affirms both those values and the rule of law, allowing families to once again move forward toward reunification."

Another plaintiff is African Communities Together, a Harlem-based nonprofit. One of its leaders called the ruling "a tremendous victory for the rule of law."

"This unlawful and racist ban caused immeasurable harm, cruelly keeping families and loved ones apart," Diana Konate, deputy executive director for policy and advocacy, said in a statement. "Today, we are elated to tell our community members: this ban is no more."

Trump expands his anti-immigration agenda

President Donald Trump has imposed a growing list of immigration and travel bans mostly for people from Africa, Asia and Latin America. The State Department said Saturday that the Trump administration is "protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants," and that it would not comment on pending litigation.

At the time the policy was issued, the State Department said it had instructed consular officers to halt immigrant visa applications from the 75 countries in accordance with a broader order in November that tightened rules around potential immigrants who might become "public charges." Relying on Council of Economic Advisers data, the State Department said that more than 30 percent of households with immigrants from these countries received some form of public assistance.

A separate notice sent to all U.S. embassies and consulates said that non-immigrant visa applicants also should be "fully vetted and screened" for the possibility that they might seek public benefits in the United States.

The cable, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, noted several times that the applicant must prove they won't apply for public benefits while in the U.S., and that consular officers who suspect the applicant might apply should require them to fill out a form proving their financial bona fides.

The ruling is the latest example of the courts upending Trump's immigration agenda. In June, a federal judge struck down a Trump administration policy that made it harder for immigrants from dozens of countries to enter and stay in America - affecting elements like asylum, work permits, green cards, and citizenship applications. That judge said the policy threw countless immigrants' lives "into indeterminate legal limbo," and accused the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services of ignoring the law.

text:
Twenty migrants deported from the United States arrived in Liberia on Thursday, the first group of an eventual 1,200 deportees that the West African country says it will receive from the U.S. under a new deal.

Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren’t their own, as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say.

An estimated 11 of those agreements, nearly half the total, are with African countries and the Liberia-U.S. agreement involves one of the largest numbers of such third-country deportations

Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum-seekers to countries they fled. Authorities in Liberia have said the deportees being welcomed in their country can seek asylum there or leave if they choose.

Here’s what to know about the deportations:

Why some African countries accept deportees

Other African countries that have received third-country deportees from the U.S. include South Sudan, Eswatini, Rwanda, Ghana, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, Congo, Uganda, Sierra Leone and the Central African Republic.

Some, like Ghana and Sierra Leone, are accepting deportees from their regions — in this case West Africa.

Many of the African countries approving the deals are among the worst hit by the Trump administration’s policies, including on trade, aid and migration. A good number of them also have authoritarian governments, raising questions about the lack of accountability and due process to ensure the protection of the deportees’ rights.

Details of most of the deals are never made public and some of the African nations, like Ghana’s government, have defended their actions as having been taken on humanitarian grounds.

The Trump administration had spent at least $40 million to deport about 300 migrants to countries other than their own, according to a February report by the Democratic staff of the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee. More countries have entered the deal since then.

Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi has described his country’s agreement as an “act of goodwill between partners,” without financial compensation. The deal came as Washington increased pressure on neighboring Rwanda over its support for M23 rebels, a dynamic analysts say may help explain Congo’s willingness to cooperate.

Many are asylum-seekers

Early flights to Africa included people that the U.S. said had convictions for serious crimes. But later transfers have included asylum-seekers with U.S. court orders protecting them from being returned to their home countries because they could face persecution or torture.

Many say they’ve been sent to countries with which they have no ties and where they were not told about until hours into the deportation journey.

Related | ICE finds heinous new way to spend millions and terrorize people

For instance, a gay Moroccan woman deported to Cameroon, where homosexuality is illegal, and an Iranian woman with U.S. court protection from returning to Iran who was sent to the Central African Republic.

Immigration lawyer Alma David called that an effective legal “loophole,” saying deportees can be left with “impossible choices” — remain in an unfamiliar country with little support or return to a country a U.S. judge found unsafe.

U.S. policy says that when a receiving government gives blanket diplomatic assurances that deportees won’t face persecution there, they can be removed without additional procedures, David told The Associated Press.

Conditions vary in different countries

Some of the deportees have recounted being shackled while some were held in full-body restraint straitjackets called the WRAP during flights that can sometimes last more than 16 hours.

Their conditions in the different countries vary. In Sierra Leone, the government hired private contractor Kenvah Solutions to provide housing, food and healthcare.

Related | Let’s check in on where Trump is deporting people this month

In Congo, the International Organization for Migration said it has provided “humanitarian assistance” and offered assisted voluntary return to the migrants’ home countries. But deportees told the AP their movements were tightly controlled. They were housed behind locked gates, could not leave alone and were allowed out roughly once a week accompanied by IOM staff.

In Equatorial Guinea, the AP found deportees confined in a hotel owned by the family of President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo. Migrants said they were barred from leaving, had uneven access to medical care and faced repeated pressure to return home. Twenty-five of at least 32 people held there had been sent to their home countries by May.

Deportations have led to lawsuits and human rights concerns

Rights advocates say the third-country deportation program risks violating non-refoulement, the principle barring governments from sending people to places where they face persecution or torture.

An international coalition sued Ghana in June on behalf of 27 deportees, alleging most were quickly sent to their home countries, despite U.S. protection orders, and that some were held under armed guard in military camps, hotels and airport cells.

text:
American Federation of Teachers (AFT) President Randi Weingarten promoted a nationwide back-to-school boycott of retail giant Target over the weekend because the company had not condemned ICE operations in Minnesota — the location of its headquarters — prompting criticism from education advocates and a call for federal scrutiny.

"We gave Target ample time to stand with the communities in which they operate and help their neighbors, but its silence about federal immigration abuses has been deafening," Weingarten said in a statement.

"The issue could not be more pressing: Seven months since the murders of Alex Pretti and Renée Good, masked ICE agents are still in our streets, our schools and our communities, terrorizing families in the name of Donald Trump’s illegal and immoral assault on immigrants striving for their American Dream," she continued. "That’s why we’re urging our members to avoid Target and patronize more ethical shopping alternatives this back-to-school season."

Weingarten also shared a video on Instagram, where she directed families to the AFT’s "Shop Smart, Not Target" website, which maps local back-to-school shopping alternatives. The organization launched the campaign Wednesday after sending Target CEO Michael Fiddelke letters in February and March.

WATCH: WEINGARTEN GESTURES WILDLY DURING ANTI-TRUMP RANT, LATER SAYS HE DRIVES HER TO DRINK

In a statement to Fox News Digital, DHS rejected the AFT's characterization of ICE.

"ICE enforces federal immigration laws, protects public safety, and conducts enforcement pursuant to federal laws and applicable agency policies. Target is not a sensitive location," an ICE spokesperson said. "However, the current policy provides guidance for officers and recognizes that enforcement actions in or near protected areas require consideration of the circumstances and applicable law. ICE will continue to conduct lawful actions wherever necessary to protect the American people."

The spokesperson further said that ICE did not target schools and called AFT's statement a false narrative.

"This is just another false narrative to try and demonize our brave ICE law enforcement, who are facing a 1,300% increase in assaults against them and an 8,000% increase in death threats," the spokesperson said.

"ICE is not going to schools to arrest children—we are protecting children. Criminals are no longer able to hide in America’s schools to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement and instead trusts them to use common sense. If a dangerous illegal alien felon were to flee into a school, or a child sex offender is working as an employee, there may be a situation where an arrest is made to protect public safety," they said.

"ICE’s position remains straightforward: its officers enforce the immigration laws enacted by Congress and carry out the agency’s mission to protect national security and public safety. ICE is engaged in targeted law enforcement operations to apprehend and remove aliens in the country unlawfully and will continue to do so despite grandstanding by politicians and criminal illegal alien supporters," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Aliens placed into removal proceedings receive due process. Once it is exhausted, ICE carries out the removal order. Dangerous rhetoric from politicians and activists demonizing our brave ICE officers has led to the over 8,000% increase in threats against DHS law enforcement who are heroically performing their congressionally mandated mission to remove criminal illegal aliens from communities across the country."

TEACHERS UNION FACING YEARS OF DEFICITS SEEKS TO BECOME OREGON'S LARGEST PAC, INTERNAL DOCUMENTS SHOW

Corey DeAngelis, a Heritage Foundation research fellow, told Fox News Digital Sunday that using the organization’s pension influence against Target raised fiduciary concerns and warranted a federal investigation.

"This partisan war on Target smells like a breach of fiduciary duty given that AFT members’ pension funds own 6.79 million shares of Target stock, which Weingarten has already leveraged to pressure the company into opposing ICE," he said. "The Department of Justice should open an investigation into the AFT using their pension funds and political influence to bully companies into falling in line with their socialist agenda."

"Urging educators and families to avoid Target is not an appropriate use of the union’s resources or influence," he added.

This isn't the AFT's first time batting against the retail giant.

DeAngelis also supplied Fox News Digital with a chart tracking Target’s closing share price against several AFT actions, including Weingarten’s letters and the organization’s March boycott resolution.

Sonja Shaw, a candidate for California superintendent of public instruction and Chino Valley Unified School District board president, told Fox News Digital on Sunday that labor leaders were prioritizing political power while students continued to struggle academically.

"Teachers’ unions are supposed to fight for teachers. Instead, union leadership has become a political machine obsessed with money, power and influence while our children continue to fall behind," she said. "In California, more than half our students are not proficient in basic reading and math. When a system produces those results year after year, that isn’t success. That’s education malpractice."

California's latest statewide assessments showed 48.8% of students met or exceeded English language arts standards and 37.3% met or exceeded math standards.

The AFT's March resolution explicitly called the effort a boycott and urged its 1.8 million members, families and allies to avoid Target until the company stood with the Twin Cities.

DeAngelis’ request followed the July appeal by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., for the Labor Department to investigate whether AFT leaders coordinated with retirement-plan fiduciaries to use members’ assets for political objectives.

House lawmakers separately demanded answers about reports that member dues helped finance Weingarten’s book, "Why Fascists Fear Teachers," while she received royalties.

Teachers spend an average of $895 of their own money every year on supplies their students need, according to a 2025 teacher spending survey.

title: Cuban and Other Trump Deportees Sent to 'Do Not Travel' African Nation Say: 'We Cannot Leave'
description:
Dozens of foreign nationals deported from the United States have found themselves stranded in the conflict-ridden Central African Republic under expanding third-country deportation agreements.
The controversial practice of sending deportees to unstable third countries has intensified legal and humanitarian scrutiny surrounding modern immigration enforcement.
Deportees living in temporary housing in Bangui explain that they have no practical way to leave the country.
Separation From Families and Children The human cost of these third-country removals is deeply felt by families remaining in the United States.
Do you believe the United States should be allowed to deport individuals to third countries if returning them to their home nation poses a threat to their safety?
text:
Dozens of foreign nationals deported from the United States have found themselves stranded in the conflict-ridden Central African Republic under expanding third-country deportation agreements.

Men from nations including Cuba, Eritrea, Ecuador, Honduras, Serbia, Russia, and Vietnam report arriving in the impoverished African nation with no prior notice, no local ties, and no identification documents. Many of these individuals had lived in the United States for years, establishing families and securing legal protections against deportation to their home countries due to fears of torture or persecution.

Now trapped in the capital city of Bangui, the deportees describe navigating severe economic hardship, language barriers, and profound separation from their loved ones.

The controversial practice of sending deportees to unstable third countries has intensified legal and humanitarian scrutiny surrounding modern immigration enforcement.

A Sudden Arrival in an Unfamiliar Land

Immigrants transported across the globe express shock and confusion after being relocated to one of the most volatile regions in the world.

For Cuban national Yasmany Moreno de Armas, the journey began after living and working in Florida for nearly a decade. Following an arrest by immigration authorities over expired parole status, the 31-year-old spent approximately a year in federal custody before discovering he had been flown directly to the Central African Republic.

The landlocked nation currently faces severe armed conflict and political instability, prompting the U.S. State Department to maintain a Level 4 travel advisory urging Americans not to visit.

Deportees living in temporary housing in Bangui explain that they have no practical way to leave the country. Moreno de Armas shared that he had never even heard of the nation prior to his arrival and now struggles with having no identification papers or financial resources.

The abrupt relocation has left many feeling effectively stateless in an environment where they cannot speak the local language or contact legal representation easily.

Separation From Families and Children

The human cost of these third-country removals is deeply felt by families remaining in the United States.

Eritrean native Zena Gebrgzabher was also among those sent to the African nation after years of building a stable life in Maryland. Working as a commercial truck driver, Gebrgzabher lived alongside his wife and their five-year-old son, both of whom are American citizens.

His sudden removal occurred during a routine check-in with immigration officials, leaving his young family devastated and struggling to explain his absence to their child.

His wife described the deportation as profoundly unfair, noting that their young son constantly asks when his father will return home. Because Gebrgzabher has no personal connections or relatives in the region, his family remains deeply concerned for his physical safety.

The emotional strain is compounded by the fact that neither man had a serious criminal record beyond immigration and minor traffic violations.

Legal Loopholes and Third-Country Pacts

The deportations highlight how bilateral agreements allow authorities to circumvent standard deportation barriers.

Under federal immigration policy, the government has established agreements with more than thirty nations to accept foreign deportees. These third-country pacts are frequently utilized when an immigrant's home nation limits or refuses repatriation flights, or when an individual has won specific protections in immigration court.

In Gebrgzabher's case, an immigration judge granted him protection under the Convention Against Torture in 2017, which legally barred authorities from returning him to Eritrea due to past military conscription and detention. However, that ruling did not grant formal permanent asylum, leaving a legal opening for officials to remove him to a third nation instead.

Similarly, Moreno de Armas faced documented risks of persecution in Cuba for previously attempting to flee the island, making third-country transfer a mechanism to execute removal orders despite local dangers.

Humanitarian Concerns and Legal Precedents

Advocates and affected individuals argue that transferring immigrants to third countries creates unacceptable safety and ethical risks.

Immigration attorneys and human rights observers warn that sending individuals to nations experiencing civil strife exposes them to severe physical dangers. The lack of consular representation, local integration programs, or basic travel documentation leaves deportees highly vulnerable to exploitation and violence in unfamiliar environments.

Both Moreno de Armas and Gebrgzabher emphasized that deportation policies should focus on returning individuals to their homelands rather than displacing them into foreign cultures.

As additional countries enter third-country agreements, legal challenges are expected to test whether sending protected individuals to conflict zones complies with international humanitarian standards.

Question for you. Do you believe the United States should be allowed to deport individuals to third countries if returning them to their home nation poses a threat to their safety?

text:
Regarding “A physics graduate, a soccer player, a teen who couldn’t swim: They died in the Ceuta migrant surge” (News, SFChronicle.com, Aug. 18): We need more stories like this that show the humanity of immigrants. What are their names? Why did they take such risks?

The story details the death of Ayoub Akbili, who was educated but poorly paid and needed money for his mother’s surgery. He was more than just another body in the crush of men flailing in the sea, trying to get somewhere for a chance at a better life. He was a human being who lost everything while trying to take care of his mother. Who wouldn’t want a son like that?

I have talked to a few immigrants over the years, gardeners from Mexico, who have shared their often harrowing stories of getting here so they can work. Their lives were stagnated, or even endangered, in their home countries. They want what all people want: a chance to succeed, to have pride in working hard to achieve it. They want their children to have opportunities they never had.

Being aware of the suffering around the world and simply turning away is harmful to our mental health. We are far better off when we maintain our compassion and understanding as we strive to manage the flow of migrants who only want a quality of life that we enjoy here in America.

Teri Shikany, Danville

Honor S.F. baseball legends

Regarding “Remember Lefty and Horace” (Letters to the Editor, Aug. 20): Lefty O’Doul and Horace Stoneham were critical to baseball in San Francisco. We cannot allow them to be forgotten.

O’Doul is a San Francisco legend, not just for the eponymous restaurant that was at Union Square for nearly 60 years, but also for his contributions to baseball in the city. After his playing days ended, he managed the San Francisco Seals of the Pacific Coast League from 1935 to 1951. O’Doul managed a young Joe DiMaggio for a year before the future Hall of Famer went to the Yankees.

text:
President Donald Trump's immigration agenda suffered another legal setback on Friday after a federal judge struck down an administration policy that suspended the processing of immigrant visas for people from 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia.

The ruling is the latest in a series of court defeats for the administration's immigration policies. It follows a June decision in which a federal judge blocked another Trump administration measure that made it harder for immigrants from dozens of countries to obtain asylum, work permits, green cards and citizenship benefits.

The decision marks another challenge to Trump's efforts to tighten immigration restrictions during his second term. The affected countries span Africa, Asia, Europe and the Middle East, potentially impacting thousands of people seeking to immigrate to the United States.

Read More on News

The case also raises questions about the extent of executive branch authority over visa policy and whether broad nationality-based restrictions can be imposed without explicit congressional authorization.

What Happened?

U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas in New York vacated the State Department policy, ruling that Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority when he ordered consular officials to stop processing immigrant visas from 75 countries whose nationals the administration deemed more likely to require public assistance in the United States.

Vargas wrote that the policy was "contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority" and conflicted with the Immigration and Nationality Act. She found that Congress gave consular officers the responsibility to determine visa eligibility on an individual basis rather than through blanket restrictions tied to nationality.

According to the ruling, the policy "categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant," undermining the statutory framework established by Congress.

Countries Affected

The policy applied to nationals of 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia, among others. The Trump administration had argued that immigrants from those nations were more likely to rely on public assistance programs after arriving in the United States.

Legal Challenge

The lawsuit was brought by two nonprofit organizations along with 11 individuals affected by the restrictions. Plaintiffs included people whose relatives had been denied visas as well as foreign nationals seeking to immigrate through employment-based petitions.

Anna Gallagher, executive director of the Catholic Legal Immigration Network (CLINIC), said in a statement that the ruling may enable some families separated by the visa restrictions to continue the immigration process, saying, "We welcome this ruling because, at its heart, this case is about keeping families together."

African Communities Together, another plaintiff in the case, described the decision as "a tremendous victory for the rule of law," and argued that the policy had unfairly separated families.

The State Department defended the administration's broader approach to immigration screening, saying it was focused on "protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants."

The department declined to comment on the lawsuit because litigation remains ongoing.

When the policy was first implemented, the State Department cited data indicating that more than 30 percent of households with immigrants from the affected countries received some form of public assistance. Officials said the measure was part of an effort to ensure prospective immigrants would not become a charge to the public.

What Happens Next?

The decision immediately invalidates the visa-processing restrictions unless a higher court intervenes. The administration could appeal the ruling, setting up another legal battle over the limits of presidential authority on immigration matters.

For now, the ruling represents the latest judicial obstacle for an administration that has repeatedly seen its immigration measures challenged in federal courts.

text:
A 62-year-old Mexican woman who lives in Tri-Cities spent five years searching for an attorney who could help adjust her immigration status in the United States.

She said five law firms in Washington state had already told her it wasn’t possible because she had entered the country illegally several times.

Then a friend suggested she contact immigration attorney Alexandra Lozano, who branded herself as the Abogada de los Milagros or “The Lawyer of Miracles.” Lozano claimed she could secure legal status in some of the most complicated immigration cases in the country.

“Other attorneys told me I didn’t qualify for a green card because I have a deportation order. But she said it was possible,” said “Ana, who works in agriculture. She agreed to share her story on condition the Herald not use her real name.

Ana paid about $15,000 for Lozano’s legal services in 2023, never imagining that three years later the attorney who often promoted herself alongside images of La Virgen de Guadalupe, a revered religious figure among many Mexicans, would shut down her law firm amid a fraud investigation.

Today, Lozano’s whereabouts in the U.S. are unknown to federal authorities investigating her for fraud.

Ana is one of 807 immigrants in the Tri-Cities and across Central and Eastern Washington who had reported by mid-July that they had paid thousands of dollars and were left in limbo after Lozano surrendered her law license and disappeared, according to the Central Washington Legal Aid, based in Yakima.

This region accounts for 17% of Lozano’s former clients who have contacted the law firm leading the civil complaint against her, wanting their money back and other compensation.

“And it could be more because this data is just based on people that have contacted the firm,” said Eillish Villa Malone, director of Immigration Legal Services at Central Washington Legal Aid. “We know there’s a big concentration of former clients in Central Washington because she had her office in Yakima.”

Since June 10, when Lozano closed her law office, at least 100 Tri-Citians have attended legal clinics where attorneys and legal advocates have advised them on what to do now that they no longer have legal representation, said Marichuy Alvízar, executive director of Unidos Nueva Alianza, one of the organizations providing legal assistance.

Lozano’s law firm also operated out of Tukwila and had support offices in Colombia, Mexico and Argentina, according to the civil complaint.

Across the United States, more than 35,000 clients were left without a lawyer after Lozano shut down her practice.

Nearly 54,000 immigration applications filed with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) listed Lozano’s firm as the attorney of record, according to a disciplinary notice from the Washington State Bar Association.

The three-law-firm team leading the civil complaint against Lozano estimates her payment agreements with clients total more than $400 million.

The lawsuit says the attorneys reached that estimate using Lozano’s average legal fees of about $10,000 to $15,000 per client and the number of people she represented.

How the lawsuit against Lozano began

Before her suspected fraud became public, the Washington Attorney General’s Office was investigating Lozano’s firm through July 2025 to determine if it engaged in deceptive and unfair business practices, according to documents obtained by The Seattle Times.

In April 2026, the legal team leading the civil complaint, Aric S. Bomsztyk of Tomlinson Bomsztyk Rus, Omar Barraza of Barraza Law, and Metz Law Group, launched a website announcing legal action against Lozano and asking former clients who believed they had been harmed to contact them.

After that effort began, Lozano changed the name of her firm to Luz Legal.

In early May, nine former clients filed a 50-page federal lawsuit against Ally Lozano LLC and En Solidaridad, a now-dissolved company that conducted psychological evaluations for people seeking to adjust their immigration status.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington, accuses Lozano of legal malpractice, breach of contract and fiduciary duty and violation of the Consumer Protection Act.

It was filed while Lozano was also under investigation by the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Shortly afterward, on May 26, Lozano gave up her law license while facing a disciplinary hearing before the Washington State Bar Association over alleged professional misconduct.

By giving up her law license, Lozano is no longer allowed to practice law in any state or remain affiliated with the law firm she founded, said Sara Niegowski, a spokesperson for the Washington State Bar Association.

In a statement published on June 10, Luz Legal, Alexandra Lozano’s law firm, said it was forced to shut down after facing what it described as unfair scrutiny in recent years.

The firm said a team of attorneys “who may have worked on your case” is available to represent former clients and it would send former clients a copy of their case files within 60 days. “Although the process may take longer,” the statement reads.

Former clients who haven’t received their files can contact Luz Legal online.

The firm also said it’s reviewing cases individually to determine whether clients are eligible for a refund.

“Please note that if your case has already been filed, you may not be entitled to a refund,” the statement reads.

Tri-Cities clients speak out

The day Ana walked into Lozano’s office, she said she only remembers asking one of the firm’s employees what services they offered and how she could pay for them.

The employee told her she could apply for lawful permanent residency through the Violence Against Women Act of 1994, or VAWA, a law that provides immigration protections for victims of domestic violence by a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident who have experienced “battery or extreme cruelty.”

Those petitions made up most of the immigration cases Lozano’s firm handled, along with T visas for victims of human trafficking, according to the lawsuit filed in May.

People applying under VAWA generally don’t have to leave the United States while their case is pending, while a T visa can provide lawful immigration status to eligible trafficking victims.

Villa Malone said some asylum seekers were also affected after Lozano’s firm closed, although they don’t make up the majority of the former clients seeking legal help.

The employee told Ana the firm would charge a $10,500 legal fee, plus five additional Citizenship and Immigration Services-related costs for immigration waivers, a psychological evaluation, a medical exam and an interpreter.

“I paid $2,500 that day and then $500 a month for 21 months. I also paid the two waivers that cost $930 each and the psychologist, which cost $1,200,” Ana said, while holding the checklist of documents she had been told to gather for her case.

“When I found out she had closed her firm, I had already gone through such a stressful time that I just thought, ‘It’s in God hands.’”

Maria, a 59-year-old Mexican woman who also lives in the Tri-Cities, said she remembers receiving the same explanation from one of Lozano’s employees when she visited the office. She also asked that her real name be withheld.

She said the employee didn’t pressure her to hire the firm, but explained the law firm had other payment options after Maria said she only had $200 her husband had given her to begin the process of legalizing her status.

Another attorney had already told Maria her case would be difficult because she had a deportation order after entering the United States multiple times. To obtain legal status, she would have to leave the country for 10 years, the attorney told her during a phone call before she contacted Lozano’s firm.

Maria came to the United States from Mexico with her mother when she was 17.

In 1998, she went to Mexico because her father died. When she tried to return to her family, she was denied entry, so she crossed the border without authorization.

She has had a deportation order ever since.

“I was pregnant with my youngest son, and they wouldn’t let me back in,” she said. “Now all of my children can go to Mexico whenever they want because they were born here. But I can’t.”

Lozano’s employee told her she could pay in installments over three years if she made a $1,500 down payment. Maria paid that amount in cash with money her son gave her.

“Then I paid $350 with my credit card every month and I think I ended up paying about $13,000,” she said. “I still had seven payments left when the office closed.”

Testimony from nearly a dozen former employees cited by The Seattle Times said Lozano pressured staff to sign up more immigrant clients.

Employees allegedly received bonuses if they convinced people to sign contracts during their first visit or reached certain quotas for new clients.

The former employees also said their primary job was explaining how clients could apply for lawful permanent residency through VAWA. According to two former employees, they followed a script that described the law as covering situations in which a spouse constantly checked a person’s phone or monitored their social media accounts.

The former employees, however, said they didn’t fabricate information provided by clients.

The Washington State Bar Association said in a statement of alleged misconduct that Lozano’s firm asked clients to sign blank documents, which were later attached to immigration filings the clients had never reviewed.

While it remains unclear what false information was included in every case, attorneys who have reviewed former clients’ files said they have found domestic violence claims that were allegedly fabricated or exaggerated, involving clients’ spouses or children.

The bar association also said the firm used clients’ signatures to submit immigration forms containing false information without first allowing them to review the documents. Some of those applications were later denied.

“It’s called (signing) with a wet signature,” said Villa Malone. “So with a pen you gotta sign it and you gotta review everything. And what the firm was doing was signing things with stamped signatures, like somehow getting digitally the signature from the person and then stamping them on.”

As part of the VAWA process, applicants must undergo a psychological evaluation documenting the effects of the abuse they experienced.

Maria said she became suspicious of the psychologist who evaluated her.

“The law firm insisted that I complete my evaluation with that specific psychologist,” she said.

The psychological evaluation was conducted by En Solidaridad, a company founded by Lozano that was run by Manuel Lozano Rodriguez, whom Lozano had married several years earlier, according to records from the Washington Secretary of State cited by the Times.

Left with unanswered questions

Neither Ana nor Maria remembers whether they signed blank documents.

Ana said she has evidence of physical abuse by her husband and believes her case could still qualify for VAWA.

Maria said the abuse she experienced was verbal.

Earlier this year, president Donald Trump directed federal agencies to strengthen fraud detection in VAWA-based immigration petitions.

Neither woman knows whether Lozano, as alleged in other cases, submitted their applications with fabricated or exaggerated accounts of abuse.

Villa Malone said it’s possible that some applications filed by Lozano’s firm accurately reflected what clients reported.

“Not all the cases submitted by that firm were fraudulent. A lot of them are getting extra scrutiny, but not all of the cases are out of luck,” she said.

She urged former clients like Ana and Maria to attend a legal clinic, where they can get help filing a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request to obtain copies of every document Lozano submitted on their behalf.

“And then get a second opinion, just so they can be aware if their application is OK and ask, ‘Are there any red flags? Am I even eligible for what I applied for?’” Villa Malone suggested.

She also recommended that former clients update their mailing address with Citizenship and Immigration Services because Lozano’s firm used its office address to receive clients’ immigration mail.

Villa Malone said it’s important for former clients to find out whether they have an upcoming immigration court hearing. Missing a hearing could further damage their cases.

“Before Trump, the case would just get denied and then nothing would happen,” Villa Malone said. “But now there is a slight risk because this administration is putting denied cases into removal proceedings.”

Maria said she doesn’t know how she will pay off the debt she took on to hire Lozano. Her husband recently underwent surgery, and she has struggled to work as she continues dealing with the effects of stomach cancer diagnosed eight years ago.

Ana said a private immigration attorney told her it would cost $25,000 just to represent her at her immigration court hearing.

“I can’t afford it because it’s too much money,” she said.

Through the civil lawsuit, the three law firms leading the case are asking the court to place Lozano’s assets into a trust for the benefit of former clients who joined the lawsuit. The number of plaintiffs nearly quadrupled from May to July.

Among the assets identified in court filings is a pink-and-white Bombardier private jet valued at about $25 million, bearing the word “abogada,” which means attorney in Spanish, and the logo of a woman with long hair.

The lawsuit also identifies a multimillion-dollar real estate portfolio that includes properties in Mexico.

Maria said she doesn’t plan to join the lawsuit because Lozano also helped her obtain a work permit.

Attorneys for several former Lozano clients told the Times that receiving work permits increased their confidence in the firm and led them to recommend her to friends and relatives.

Applicants seeking lawful permanent residency are often eligible to receive temporary work authorization while their cases are pending.

Maria’s work permit expires in 2030. She said she now uses it to work in agriculture sporadically.

Michelle Carney, an immigration attorney who serves on state and national legal ethics committees, told the Times that filing a green card application for someone who doesn’t qualify can put that person at risk.

“It exposes that person to the risk of being placed into removal proceedings,” she said.

Maria said another attorney advised her to memorize her alien registration number in case she is ever detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“He told me to memorize it and send it to my children in case immigration arrests me,” she said. “With that number they can find me. I told my husband, ‘I can’t do anything if they deport me.’ My children are grown now. Thank God they can go to Mexico.”

Ana also received a work permit and is currently using it.

When she attended a legal clinic in Richland in late July, she said she wasn’t interested in joining the civil lawsuit.

“Where can I go to tell my story?” she asked two weeks later.

text:
Secretary Mullin explained the change as an attempt to protect national security and prevent immigration fraud.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has been sued by a coalition of university organizations and labor unions after the agency ended the “duration of status” policy for international students studying in the U.S. on student visas. Under the new rule, foreign students will be limited to four-year stays and required to undergo a federal review that includes submitting biometric information and security, identity, and fraud screening if an extension is needed.

When the policy update was announced, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “For nearly half a century, the outdated ‘duration of status’ system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud. For decades, foreign students have been admitted into the U.S. indefinitely, allowing thousands to abuse our immigration system by perpetually enrolling in courses to avoid having to leave the U.S.“

The plaintiffs have requested a preliminary injunction to halt the rule from being implemented, claiming it will place significant administrative burdens on both international students and the institutions that support them.

text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ohio — Springfield residents and advocates are reacting to reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and arrests in the city over the last week, including the detention of a local pastor described by a faith group as a prominent member of the Haitian community.

The mayor of Springfield has confirmed ICE’s presence in the city. ICE has previously said that it does not comment on ongoing operations.

G92, a faith group in Springfield, said one of the people detained, Gilbert Joubert Adrien, was a local pastor and a well-known religious leader in the Haitian community.

“He’s well-known and regarded in the Haitian community,” G92 spokesperson Michael McCrelland said. “He’s a religious leader, which in any community is important, but particularly so among the Haitians. And to snatch him up like ICE has done is just a gut punch to the people who are trying to barely get by here already.”

Advocates said ICE’s presence has had a broader effect on the Haitian community. In an interview with Spectrum News earlier in August, James Pepitho Fleurijean, with the Haitian Support Center, said some people were afraid to leave their homes or open their businesses.

“As you can tell, most of the Haitian business, they are all closed,” Fleurijean said. “The restaurant, the stores, everything they shut down completely. And the people are not really coming out.”

At least one Haitian restaurant in the area was closed outside its typical hours, though the exact reason was unknown. Kevin Bonecutter said he drove from Cincinnati to support the restaurant but found it empty.

“It’s just like a dagger right into my heart,” Bonecutter said. “Just the belief of living in America, we should be free. We should be able to live in the streets and not be afraid of walking down the streets or coming to work and just running our own business and being detained.”

The developments come after Springfield drew national attention during the 2024 presidential debate. The city has remained a focus in national immigration discussions.

During a visit Friday, Republican Vice President JD Vance received applause from some attendees as he discussed deportation efforts and job growth.

“For the first time in my life, America saw net migration out of the country as we sent millions of illegal immigrants back home,” Vance said.

Vance also said he was proud of job growth among native-born Americans.

“As a result of that, this is maybe the thing I’m most proud of in the last 18 months,” Vance said. “Do you know that all net job growth over the past 18 months went to native-born Americans, reversing a trend for four years where it all went to other people?”

Ohio Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker said she disagrees with the ongoing deportation effort and supports the Haitian community remaining in Springfield.

“I welcome the Haitian community because they should feel safe there,” Knickerbocker said. “They are not safe if they go home to Haiti. And so it is important for those that are willing to contribute to our society, build businesses, pay taxes, that they get to remain here.”

It is not known how long ICE will continue operating in Springfield. Haitian immigrants lost their temporary protected status earlier this year.

text:
Afghan Voice Agency (AVA): This policy, which took effect on January 21 of this year, suspended the issuance of immigrant visas for citizens of countries including Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia, Bosnia and Albania, and a number of countries in Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean. The US State Department cited the “high risk of applicants becoming a financial burden on the government” as the reason for this action.

In his ruling, Judge Vargas ruled that the Immigration and Nationality Act does not allow the Secretary of State to block visas based solely on an applicant’s nationality. He said that the assessment of each applicant’s potential financial burden must be made on an individual basis, taking into account factors such as age, family status, assets, education and skills. The judge, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, called the policy a “direct violation” of the legal framework established by Congress.

The ruling was issued in response to a lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups including the Catholic Immigration Legal Network and African Communities Together, as well as a number of visa applicants and U.S. citizens who sponsored family members from countries covered by the policy.

Under the ruling, the State Department can no longer deny or block immigrant visa applications based solely on the applicant’s nationality, and cases must be reviewed on an individual basis. However, this ruling does not mean that other restrictions on entry to the United States or the immediate issuance of visas for all applicants will be lifted, and each case must still meet its legal requirements.

It is worth noting that the Trump administration has imposed extensive restrictions on immigration during its second term in office, which has faced legal backlash and criticism from human rights groups. These groups believe that some of these policies violate the legal rights of immigrants and lead to racial discrimination. The US State Department has not responded to the ruling by the time this news was published.

title: ICE has not delivered the more humane tactics it promised - The Des Moines Register
description:
But with DHS’s recently announced plans for ICE officers to wear “electric shock gloves,” literally nothing could be further from the truth.
The New York Times reported a 276% daily increase in Iowa ICE arrests in the first five months of last year.
In Iowa ICE detained 1,779 people, of which 1,533 were deported.
Peggy Flanagan, whose city and state lived through some of the worst ICE tactics, called it outrageous to introduce a new tool of violence.
ICE arrested 10,000 people over five days in late June, at such check-ins, traffic stops and on the street.
text:
Rekha Basu is a longtime syndicated columnist, editorial writer, reporter and author of the book, “Finding Your Voice.”

She retired in 2022 as a Des Moines Register columnist.

When Markwayne Mullin replaced Kristi Noem as Department of Homeland Security secretary, some news media described his pledge for a “softer touch” on immigration enforcement. But with DHS’s recently announced plans for ICE officers to wear “electric shock gloves,” literally nothing could be further from the truth.

Planned for early next year, those gloves, when activated, will stun those migrants into cooperating ― at a cost to taxpayers of up to $20 million. “Recipients don’t pass out but the pain can compel them to cooperate with officers,” USA Today reported. "The glove causes pain and distraction through sustained physical contact.”

They’re not meant to be used for punishment or on children, the elderly, disabled or pregnant people (how would they know who might be pregnant?), according to the manufacturer’s manual. But they can be used to coerce someone out of a car or a home or into jail.

In Iowa, stopping motorists, even for minor infractions, is often the first step in immigrant apprehension, whether or not that’s what they were stopped for. According to the nonprofit Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, “Iowa drivers are being stopped for minor traffic violations before being transferred over to ICE. The data shows that often, this is how people enter the deportation pipeline from Iowa.”

An IMMJ report accuses the Trump administration of “actively hiding data about its deportation actions in our community and across the country.” But information released last month by the University of California Berkeley’s Deportation Data Project says ICE arrests made on the streets, in immigration courts and routine appointments increased 11-fold in Trump’s first year back in office. Overall, its arrests quadrupled. The New York Times reported a 276% daily increase in Iowa ICE arrests in the first five months of last year. In Iowa ICE detained 1,779 people, of which 1,533 were deported. The vast majority of detainees were male and 63% were citizens of Mexico or Guatemala.

Eight Iowa county jails ― Woodbury, Pottawattamie, Polk, Hardin, Linn, Muscatine, Sioux, Scott and Marion ― have agreements to detain people on behalf of ICE for 72 hours or more. If that weren’t bad enough, local and state police will be, in Mullin’s words, taking “the front row” on ICE’s work ― with DHS acting “as more of a transport rather than on the front lines.” Under the federal program, called 287(g), local police and sheriffs get trained to take on ICE enforcement activities.

Those are the very people communities are supposed to trust for help and call in emergencies. But it can be hard to tell local police from ICE agents when they show up as masked men in unmarked cars wearing bulletproof vests labeled "police," and stop people on the street with guns, says IMMJ: “For vulnerable communities, these realities represent real terror that haunts them daily.”

Asked by CNN about the electric shock gloves, Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, whose city and state lived through some of the worst ICE tactics, called it outrageous to introduce a new tool of violence. “This agency is completely out of control,” she told CNN.

The shock gloves of course aren’t the worst threat facing immigrants, but they’re a reflection of the inhumanity with which this administration views and treats those here without proper papers, many of whom are filling jobs others won’t. The DHS website says the gloves are designed “to safely arrest and remove criminal aliens from our country.” But deportation is, or should be, a process involving pleas, attorneys and scheduled hearings, not achieved by throwing an electrified leash on someone and transferring them to a holding pen.

All of this is rationalized in the name of safety, though it doesn’t offer any. To attract local police participation, DHS claims, “It helps you keep your community safe from potentially dangerous criminal aliens.”

But since Trump took office, the word “criminal” to describe undocumented people has become almost meaningless. Merely being here without a visa is not a criminal offense but a civil infraction. Someone may be placed in removal proceedings and charged a fine, but it’s not a federal crime.

Someone caught while entering the U.S. without permission can be criminally charged, as can a person who was ordered deported but stayed or re-entered without authority. But since Trump’s return to office, even people attending check-ins with immigration officials are getting nabbed and deported. ICE arrested 10,000 people over five days in late June, at such check-ins, traffic stops and on the street.

Mullin has said, “My goal in six months is that we're not in the lead story every single day.” So much for that. In other related moves recently:

A new federal requirement makes every noncitizen 14 or older register with the federal government within 30 days of entering and provide fingerprints and home addresses so they can be tracked. Even foreigners here lawfully who didn’t register or weren’t carrying their permanent residence cards have been handcuffed and hauled off.

Mullin is threatening to stop international air traffic from arriving at “sanctuary cities,” which include Chicago, Los Angeles, and New York City. That would mean visas couldn’t be processed in those major transportation hubs.

Federal agents in Minnesota have launched “Operation Puppet Master,” an undercover surveillance of progressive organizations, labor unions and groups protesting the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. Fifteen people were charged with helping “violent opportunists and agitators.” The operation became public when a defense lawyer made a motion for the release of materials the government collected.

ICE is arresting people at airports who have open immigration cases and no criminal history ― apparently to meet the administration’s goal of 3,000 deportations a day.

During traffic stops, ICE agents in one recent week. shot and killed two people, one in Texas who they believed to be someone else, and the other in Maine, who they said had a removal order.

Whether or not it makes the headlines, multiple such stories play out every day. “ICE’s detentions and deportations are collectively impacting all immigrants and refugees in Iowa,” says IMMJ. They may include the people who clean your hotel room, farm your land, fix your roof or care for your aging parents or kids.

But there are steps you can take: Stand by those migrants under threat. Attend an IMMJ training. Research the candidates’ positions on this horrific seizure of our streets and communities. And use your vote in November’s midterm elections to end these abhorrent, and shocking, practices.

title: 'Unworthy of trust': Is Trump pushing the Justice Department too far? - USA Today
description:
But Justice Department lawyers, bound by the facts and law in carrying out his priorities, have struggled to fulfill his aggressive rhetoric amid an explosion of litigation.
Government lawyers have acknowledged violating dozens of court orders in immigration cases.
As the back-and accumulates, the credibility of Justice Department lawyers are facing scrutiny.
'Not vandalism': Prosecutors drop Reflecting Pool charges Trump was a vocal advocate for pursuing vandalism charges over damage to the Reflecting Pool’s liner on the National Mall.
Overall, Fox acknowledged the government violated court orders 56 times in 547 cases during that two-month period.
text:
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump can – and does – say anything he wants on social media to spur criminal investigations of perceived rivals and his immigration crackdown. But Justice Department lawyers, bound by the facts and law in carrying out his priorities, have struggled to fulfill his aggressive rhetoric amid an explosion of litigation.

Grand juries have refused to indict suspects and prosecutors dropped charges in high-profile cases. Government lawyers have acknowledged violating dozens of court orders in immigration cases. And judges have accused government lawyers of misrepresenting the facts in some civil cases.

As the back-and accumulates, the credibility of Justice Department lawyers are facing scrutiny. Judges are questioning whether the lawyers are reliable, under what is called the “presumption of regularity,” and have begun asking for sworn statements to accompany court filings.

“We’ve seen a lot of judges saying that the federal government is not entitled to a presumption of regularity,” said Josh Blackman, a professor at South Texas College of Law in Houston. “I think that we’re going to see judges start not giving DOJ the benefit of the doubt.”

Legal experts said the disconnect between Trump's advocacy and what holds up in court erodes confidence in the department.

“A lot of it is pressure coming from the top, whether it is President Trump or senior officials within the Justice Department,” Stephen Yale-Loehr, a retired immigration-law professor at Cornell, told USA TODAY. “It undermines the American public’s faith in the Justice Department.”

Drawing broad conclusions from decisions in specific cases is difficult. Government lawyers have said mistakes were inadvertent. And some of the conflicts are political. A Justice Department spokesperson said multiple District Court judges opposed administration policies “before eventually relenting,” as in cases about ending temporary protections for immigrants from deportation.

“Investigative and prosecutorial decisions are made based on the law and the facts,” Kiersten Pels told USA TODAY.

'Not vandalism': Prosecutors drop Reflecting Pool charges

Trump was a vocal advocate for pursuing vandalism charges over damage to the Reflecting Pool’s liner on the National Mall. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for DC, charged Olympian David Hearn in July and accused him of “damaging a national resource, a national treasure.”

But Pirro’s office dropped the charges and acknowledged he Department of the Interior found “the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism,” according to a July 31 filing in DC Superior Court. Trump said she "choked."

Simply securing indictments has been difficult. Trump pressed publicly for charges against former FBI Director James Comey, who had investigated him, and New York Attorney General Letitia James, who won a $500 million civil judgment against him. Trump called Democratic lawmakers “traitors” and “seditious” for saying soldiers don't need to follow illegal orders.

But a judge threw out charges against Comey for allegedly lying to Congress and against James for alleged bank fraud by ruling the prosecutor was appointed unlawfully. Comey still faces charges in another case of threatening the president with a picture of seashells, which he denies. A grand jury refused to indict the targeted lawmakers.

The government also failed to get a felony indictment against Sean Dunn, the man who threw a Subway sandwich at a Customs and Border Protection agent during a surge in immigration enforcement. The department then took a misdemeanor case against him to trial, which it lost.

'Roller coaster' of criminal charges filed and dropped in DC: judge

U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui called the government’s handling of criminal cases in DC “unprecedented” for pursuing charges by complaint after grand juries refused to indict, charging cases with “apparent constitutional violations” and “rushing to charge cases before properly investigating them.”

Statistics helped tell the story. Faruqui found the government dismissed 20 cases out of more than 4,000 filed by complaint in DC from 2014 to 2024. But during eight weeks late 2025, the government dismissed 20 cases out of 95 charged by complaint.

“For the last several weeks, judges in this District have seen case after case involving unprecedented prosecutorial action,” Faruqui wrote in an October 2025 order. “Arresting, charging, dismissing, re-charging, dismissing again, recharging again in another court, and dismissing again: this roller coaster is anything but normal.”

Suzanne Goldberg, a professor at Columbia Law School, said the pace of filings could offer a partial explanation. She also said the department lost a "startling" number of experienced lawyers as a result of terminations and resignations, which could have hurt the vetting of cases.

“But this volume of dropped charges suggests that the department is either intentionally charging when they do not have a good case because they want people to feel threatened or it is not doing the most basic work required to vet charges before filing," Goldberg, a former official in the State and Education departments in the Biden administration, told USA TODAY.

How big a problem is birth tourism? 'No one knows for sure.'

Trump made restrictions on birthright citizenship a top priority. He signed an executive order on his first day of his second term. He became the first sitting president to attend a Supreme Court argument about the order.

But the administration's lawyer had to tread cautiously when Chief Justice John Roberts asked at the April 1 argument: “Do you have any information about how common that is or how significant a problem it is?”

Solicitor General John Sauer cited news reports than 1 million people in China or more could be U.S. citizens and hundreds of companies cater to “birth tourism.”

But Sauer prefaced his estimates by saying: “It's a great question. No one knows for sure.”

Judges find possible contempt, abuse of power in Kilmar Abrego Garcia deportation

As part of his immigration crackdown, Trump invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to speed deportations of alleged terrorists. But the strategy quickly hit a hurdle when Kilmar Abrego Garcia, an immigrant from El Salvador, was mistakenly deported in March 2025 despite having an immigration court order allowing him to remain in the United States.

U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, who was appointed by Barack Obama, ruled the government disregarded his order blocking the deportation flight. He found probable cause for criminal contempt, with boasts by government officials “intimated they had defied the Court’s Order deliberately and gleefully.”

But the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals halted Boasberg’s contempt inquiry. Trump has called Boasberg a “disgrace” and “Out of Control.”

The government returned Abrego Garcia but charged him in Tennessee with alleged human smuggling. U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw, who was also appointed by Obama, dismissed the charges in May as “an abuse of prosecuting power.”

'Beyond the pale': Minnesota judge on violations of court orders

Trump, who campaigned on border security and threatened to deport all undocumented immigrants, promotes the highest detention rates on record. But the enforcement surge flooded federal courts with litigation.

In Minnesota, U.S. Chief District Judge Patrick Schiltz got into a spat with U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen about how many times Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers violated judicial orders.

Schiltz, who was appointed by George W. Bush, noted “grave concerns” Feb. 26 after “extraordinarily busy judges” counted 96 violations in 74 cases in January alone. Rosen disputed the findings.

“Assuming the statistical sample we chose is as representative of the whole as I believe it likely is, the information compiled by others for your order was far beyond the pale of accuracy for an order that would be wielded so publicly and so sharply,” Rosen wrote the judge on Feb. 9. "The lawyers in my civil division didn’t deserve it."

So the judge sharpened his pencil and checked the figures again. Schiltz said “the bottom line is that ICE violated 97 orders in 66 of the cases” in January. He also found “113 additional orders that ICE has violated in 77 additional cases” through the end of February.

“If anything is ‘beyond the pale,’ it is ICE’s continued violation of the orders of this Court,” Schiltz wrote. “Increasingly, this Court has had to resort to using the threat of civil contempt to force ICE to comply with orders.”

'Mistakes can be made': New Jersey judge

In New Jersey, U.S. District Judge Michael Farbiarz, who was appointed by Joe Biden, blocked the government from moving a detained immigrant on Jan. 26. But government lawyers notified him the detainee was flown to a Texas detention center on Jan. 31 anyway. The detainee was returned on Feb. 5.

Jordan Fox, chief of staff and associate deputy attorney general, acknowledged that 17 detainees had been transferred mistakenly from Dec. 5, 2025, to Feb. 12, 2026, after judges blocked their removals. All were returned to New Jersey, he said. Overall, Fox acknowledged the government violated court orders 56 times in 547 cases during that two-month period.

“We will continue to act with the utmost vigilance to prevent, self-report, and ensure compliance with court orders during this unprecedented period of immigration filings in one of the hardest hit districts in the country,” Fox wrote. “Adherence to court orders is a bedrock feature of our justice system; ensuring that adherence is a core responsibility of our Office.”

Farbiarz weighed holding officials in criminal contempt for transfer violations averaging more than once per week.

“An email might not be forwarded here or there. Work pressures build and it can be hard to dig out. Mistakes can be made,” Farbiarz wrote. “But when the same mistakes happen over and over again – the picture can start to look different.”

DOJ 'unworthy' of trust: Rhode Island judge

Disputes about investigative subpoenas led judges to increasingly question what they are told by Justice Department lawyers, whether investigating transgender care, Air Force One security or the 2020 election.

“I know that many judges have declined to give DOJ lawyers the presumption of regularity, that is, benefit of the doubt that they have done their jobs properly and that their representations can be trusted,” Barb McQuade, a University of Michigan law professor and former U.S. attorney, told USA TODAY. “In the long term, an erosion of that presumption of regularity can make it more difficult for Justice Department lawyers to do their jobs if judges don't trust them when they speak in court.”

Trump has campaigned for years against transgender surgery for children and demanded legislation aiming to ban it. But government lawyers ran into a hornet’s nest after subpoenaing Rhode Island hospital for records about medical care for gender dysphoria.

U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy, who was appointed by Trump, revoked the subpoena after criticizing federal prosecutors for withholding information and misrepresenting facts in a case about the treatment of gender dysphoria. She said “the discrepancy between the honorable conduct expected of federal prosecutors and DOJ’s tactics in this case is unsettling.”

“DOJ has proven unworthy of this trust at every point in this case,” McElroy wrote. “Its representatives have, under oath, misrepresented salient facts.”

Subpoena for info about Georgia election workers 'unreasonable': judge

Trump has continued to assert without evidence he won the 2020 election and he has urged broad investigations of alleged fraud, including an FBI search of records in Fulton County, Georgia.

But U.S. District Judge William Ray, who was appointed by Trump, blocked a Justice Department subpoena he called “unreasonable” and "staggering."

The government sought personal information from thousands of poll workers and volunteers from the 2020 election in Fulton County even though Ray said too many years have passed to pursue criminal charges.
