text:
Every Congress for the past 25 years, Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., has introduced the DREAM Act, a bill that would provide a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants who came to the U.S. as children. Now, as his congressional career comes to an end, Durbin is looking for someone to inherit his signature issue.

There may not be one person. But there will certainly be someone.

“Several people have asked,” Durbin told MS NOW.

He said Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., and Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., are strong candidates to take the lead on the DREAM Act, but “there are others that are interested as well.”

“So I hope they put together a strong team,” Durbin said.

The Development, Relief and Education for Alien Minors Act has been a major Democratic priority for 25 years, ever since Durbin and the late Republican Sen. Orrin Hatch, R-Utah, first cosponsored the legislation in 2001.

Although some versions of the bill have garnered as many as 48 cosponsors in the Senate over the years, the measure has never passed the upper chamber and has been losing steam in recent years, as both parties have taken a harder line over immigration. The closest lawmakers ever got to enacting the legislation was in 2010, when the bill passed the House and the Senate voted 55-41 to advance it, falling five votes short of the 60 needed to overcome a filibuster.

While the vote was mainly split along party lines, five Democrats voted against the legislation, meaning the DREAM Act could have passed if those senators had supported the bill. Three Republican senators, after all, voted for the measure.

But since 2010, bipartisan support for the DREAM Act has been harder to find. Republicans who once cosponsored the legislation have long since distanced themselves from it, as “pathway to citizenship” becomes a forbidden phrase in the GOP.

And without sufficient Republican support, some Democrats have been hesitant to open themselves up to criticism for backing the legislation themselves. It has led Durbin to an increasingly fruitless — though not entirely lonely — pursuit to pass the DREAM Act.

Indeed, the DREAM Act has become synonymous with Durbin. He has made the legislation the defining issue of his 44-year career in Congress.

Now, with Durbin — the No. 2 Democrat in the Senate — leaving Congress at the end of the year, the DREAM Act is facing an even tougher path to passage. But that is not the only blow to the measure.

While Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., did not support the bill in 2010, he later repeatedly teamed up with Durbin on the legislation. Graham was the primary cosponsor for the bill in 2017, 2019, 2021 and 2023.

Even though Graham pulled his support this Congress, Durbin clearly saw an opening with his South Carolina colleague — particularly if the immigration issue ever cooled down on the Republican side.

Now, with Graham gone, Durbin is looking to his replacement — Graham’s sister, Darline Graham — as a possible new Republican partner.

Durbin told MS NOW he actually has hope of converting the newly appointed senator.

“She’s new,” Durbin told MS NOW. “I’ll let her settle in a little bit. I will talk to her.”

That may be a difficult sell, if Darline Graham even wins the race to replace her brother. As Durbin knows, the GOP’s growing opposition to the DREAM Act is emblematic of the issue’s broader political problem.

For years, Durbin could point to a handful of Republicans who were willing to cross party lines for the legislation. But now, his bipartisan coalition has shrunk, and he is leaving the Senate with the DREAM Act in a tough spot.

Recommended

Not that Durbin has failed to make progress on the legislation throughout his career.

In 2012, Durbin worked alongside then-President Barack Obama — once his close Senate partner from Illinois — to create the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, known as DACA, providing temporary protection to people who were brought to the U.S. as children.

But since the start of the second Trump administration, people with protected DACA status have been the target of new enforcement actions, including deportation efforts even when the status of some of those DACA recipients had not expired.

In June, Padilla and Cortez Masto joined Durbin and Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., on a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche raising legal concerns with the Justice Department’s decision to weaken DACA protections — another signal of who may take the reins on the DREAM Act when Durbin departs.

As Democrats know, the Trump administration’s actions have made it much harder to pass the DREAM Act. Even if the bill could get through Congress, Trump would almost certainly veto the legislation.

But Durbin says the DREAM Act still has some support inside the Republican conference — even if that support is mostly private. He told MS NOW that several GOP senators have told him that they have “got to do this” — meaning pass the DREAM Act — and have pushed Durbin to continue advocating for the legislation.

“They understand,” Durbin said of these Republicans.

One of the few GOP senators who continues to publicly support the DREAM Act is Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska.

Murkowski cosponsored the measure with Durbin at the start of this Congress in 2025, and she told MS NOW she has been talking with different colleagues about a path forward on immigration legislation.

Murkowski said that while the Trump administration has focused on securing the border, there is a “real recognition” within Congress that lawmakers need to address legal immigration.

“While we have paid attention to those who may be coming through illegally, we have not worked to address the concerns about an immigration process that isn’t working well for so many others,” Murkowski told MS NOW. “And so what we need to do to weigh in there, those are some of the really positive talks that we’ve been having.”

Although she has been having conversations with other senators, she said they have not worked anything out in terms of timing. Murkowski also did not answer whether she plans on reintroducing the DREAM Act specifically.

Murkowski’s continued involvement could be significant. She was one of three Republicans who voted for the DREAM Act in 2010, and Durbin said he knows that supporting the DREAM Act was “tough for her politically.”

Murkowski did it anyway.

“I respect her so much for it,” Durbin told MS NOW. “I’m going to plead with her to stick with it after I’m gone.”

text:
After nearly a week, more than 140 detained people at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma have ended their hunger strike over alleged inedible and untimely food portions and medical neglect.

The strikers were promised new menus, bigger portions and better food. But as of Thursday, the changes still have not been implemented, according to advocates.

The strike began last Tuesday and involved two units of detained people, who participated for five and six days, respectively. The strikers demanded edible food, timely meals, access to hygiene items and medical care, according to advocates.

“They remain optimistic but cautious because they do not trust that GEO will actually follow through on their promises,” said Josefina Mora-Cheung, a spokesperson for La Resistencia, an advocacy organization whose members recently talked to those who were previously on strike.

GEO Group, one of the largest private incarceration companies in the U.S. and the operator of the Tacoma detention facility, is in charge of the food in the detention center. But U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is in charge of healthcare, according to a spokesperson for GEO Group.

ICE declined to comment.

The facility, about a mile away from downtown Tacoma, holds over 1,500 people and is one of the largest ICE detention centers in the country. Most of the people inside are indefinitely detained.

This is the 20th hunger strike this year at the facility.

At the facility, people have reported inadequate medical care, black mold in showers, unsafe drinking water, laundry returned wet and dirtier than before, and food containing “burned plastic, metal string, rope, splinters, hair, and worms.”

On Saturday, two members of Congress arrived at the detention center unannounced amid the strike to see the conditions of the facility.

U.S. Rep. Maxine Dexter, D-Ore., visited the center alongside U.S. Rep. Emily Randall, D-Wash., and the two were allowed to tour housing units and the kitchen, but were denied access to the medical wing or medical staff.

Dexter and Randall said many questions remained about detainees’ health and hunger concerns after the visit.

“We hope that they can help create that pressure on ICE for medical attention and services that people require for life threatening conditions,” Mora-Cheung said about the lawmakers’ visit.

Advertising

The strike also comes amid an ongoing legal battle between the state and GEO Group over health inspections. After the state passed a law in 2023 setting health and safety standards for private detention centers in the state, GEO Group has prevented health officials from inspecting the center.

The company has also faced allegations of inhumane conditions and mistreating the people in its care. In February, staff were sued for assault and sexual abuse.

“Although the legal battle continues, this hunger strike was a clear example of the need for levels of accountability that currently do not exist,” Mora-Cheung said.

text:
Following the US Supreme Court's latest ruling effectively terminating Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, for Haitian immigrants, many individuals — especially in Florida, which has the nation's largest Haitian population — are urgently looking for alternatives.

And for some, Canada is a potentially promising destination.

Haitians are urgently searching for any possible entry, from employer-sponsored permits to Express Entry programs for skilled, bilingual workers, said Cassandra Fultz, a regulated Canadian immigration consultant and founder of Doherty Fultz Immigration.

Fultz told WLRN she's "experiencing a 20-30% increase" in inquiries and applications from Haitian nationals since the end of last year.

"We were hoping that the Supreme Court might make a different decision and that this is not how things would end up," Fultz said. "But since the Supreme Court decision, the interest has increased even more. Many people are starting the process, initiating the steps, getting their documents together so that they can make a trip."

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in late June that the Trump administration can terminate TPS for about 350,000 Haitian nationals.

There are nearly 100,000 people of Haitian descent living in Canada, with the majority, nearly 90%, living in the province of Quebec, and concentrated in its city of Montréal, according to the 2021 Canadian Census.

Haitians make up the largest group of irregular migrants entering Canada, according to the latest data from the Canadian government.

Haitians who do apply for asylum are more than likely to be rejected than approved. The Immigration and Refugee Board reported that about 34% of Haitian asylum applicants were approved between 2017 and the first half of 2022.

Fultz told WLRN that U.S. work experience, along with English and French proficiency, could provide qualified applicants with a major advantage in the Canadian job market.

READ MORE: Is it a human rights violation to deport Haitian TPS holders to a cauldron of gang violence?

While a valid passport is mandatory, the specific documentation needed varies depending on whether one pursues a work permit or permanent residency.

"It's okay if you renew your passport to make the application and it's got the whole 10 years on it. Either way is fine, but you're definitely going to need a passport," Fultz said.

"Different applications have different documentary requirements. Permanent residence applications have totally different considerations from, say, like a work permit application or even a visitor visa just to get on the plane."

Permanent residency, for example, require full background checks, from education credentials and biometrics to detailed employment records.

Ultimately, the transition is facilitated by the cultural similarities between the two North American employment sectors, making employer-supported immigration a feasible path for those losing their status, she said.

"Where your U.S. work experience actually really gives you a leg up is in the employment market in Canada because Canadian work experience is, of course, the gold standard in Canada," she said.

"We're all on sort of the same wavelength in terms of employment culture, expectations, cultural employment norms."

Bilingual Haitian candidates proficient in both English and French could be particularly sought after by employers across all Canadian provinces, Fultz added.

"Not only is an employer gonna be very interested in this, there could even be a bidding war," she said.

Bilingual candidates in Canada are "the gold standard," she said.

authors: Lauren McCauley, Emma Davis, Eesha Pendharkar

We tell immigrants to follow the rules, meet the deadlines imposed upon them, file paperwork, attend hearings, said Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition.

text:
On Monday morning, I joined roughly 200 others in the Biddeford High School auditorium to witness a congressional hearing on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s use of force in the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.

As editor of a daily news site, I know too well how President Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda has been executed in states across the country, including my own. I’ve read and edited stories every day about policy changes, court battles, arrest quotas, people being snatched off the streets. You almost become numb to it.

I also have friends who are immigrants, doing everything asked of them and still living in fear that their children will come home to an empty house and parents en route to a detention center on the other side of the country.

Despite all of this knowledge, I still found myself shocked to hear about the utter disregard for human life that this shooting, and the silence that has followed, has shown.

The lie that the federal government is merely going after “criminals” who are “abusing our system” has once again been exposed and it is clear that the country is being run by people intent on terrorizing America’s immigrant population.

And those communities — our communities — are tired, and scared, and have been doing all they can to support each other. On top of being devastated by that reality, I also came away from the hearing in awe of the fact that these grassroots efforts have been able to resist those forces bent on their demise.

It is daunting, particularly with the massive infusion of funds gifted to ICE by Congress, but something that diverse panel showed is that there is a role for everyone: advocacy; legal help; providing rides, a meal or a few bucks; or even attending a “shadow” hearing in a Maine high school auditorium.

During the hearing, we heard about how on a Monday morning in July, masked federal agents descended on the southern Maine community and tried to apprehend a man who was not their target and had done nothing wrong and then shot and killed him. How they immediately fled the scene, and in the month since have provided zero information or communication with the town, the family, and the officials seeking answers and justice.

Ben Gideon, legal representation for the Guerrero family, said that neither the FBI nor the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has reached out to the family to investigate the shooting. “As far as we can tell the federal government has chosen to turn a blind eye completely,” Gideon told reporters afterwards.

Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain described how local law enforcement had to secure “the aftermath of a scene we were not permitted to investigate,” and then how the city stood up mental health and crisis support for the traumatized community of 22,500 people, many of whom have now “retreated from public life.”

He described talking with a mother who will not be sending her daughter to Kindergarten when school begins later this month.

“Federal enforcement actions do not end when agents leave,” LaFountain told the panel. “The authority was federal, the burden is local.”

We heard about how, amid a dearth of official information, reporting into the history of the suspected shooter uncovered a record of violence, raising major questions about training and vetting processes for an immigration crackdown that since July 2025 has received $240 billion in taxpayer dollars to fuel their detention and deportation operations.

“Congress cannot continue expanding power without expanding what restrains it,” LaFountain said.

LaFountain also said that if media reports are accurate, the individual “would never be hired” by Biddeford Police. He also noted that despite the less than $10 million budget, all officers wear bodycams, which was not the case with the ICE agents that day.

U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the top Democrat on the U.S. House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee, said Republicans on the committee have refused to provide any oversight of ICE, forcing Democrats to hold shadow field hearings in Houston, New Orleans, Chicago, Minneapolis, New Jersey — and now Biddeford.

We heard about how the Trump administration has cut off all legal pathways to immigration. Sue Roche, executive director of Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project, said that has created “chaos, fear and confusion” for New Mainers.

We tell immigrants to follow the rules, meet the deadlines imposed upon them, file paperwork, attend hearings, said Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition. We “tell them to live normal lives,” she said, yet 70% of people apprehended had no criminal conviction.

In Maine, federal agents have specifically targeted asylum seekers, said Roche, whose organization provides legal aid to immigrants. Even those who are detained for overstaying their visa, that is a civil infraction that Roche described as “paperwork problems” that don’t “merit a militarized response.”

“Every human has constitutional rights,” Roche said, “this administration is trying to make people forget it.”

Amid Trump administration silence, national Democrats hold ‘shadow’ hearing on fatal ICE shooting

We heard about how Maine’s immigrant community had been preparing for this since January 2025. And how that early organizing, which included establishing an ICE watch hotline and a solidarity fund, has allowed many families to shelter in place, or be freed from detention.

Since DHS launched its enhanced deportation operation in January, the hotline has fielded roughly 18,000 calls, said Chitam.

“ICE never left our state. As we speak, they are still picking people up,” she said, noting there were nearly 2,000 arrests from January to August.

Since it launched in September 2025, the Maine Solidarity Fund has raised and spent more than $1.8 million, according to Presente! Maine Executive Director Crystal Cron. In addition to providing housing and food support, the majority of this fund has been used for bonds, she said, which people are required to pay before release from detention, regardless of whether they are guilty of breaking any laws.

Initially, Cron said bonds were typically around $3,000-5,000, but now they are regularly $20,000 to $30,000. But, she noted, most immigrants picked up in Maine “have been able to come home,” which is not the case with immigrant communities in other states she’s heard from.

We also heard about how Guerrero’s shooting confirmed their worst fears.

“To say we are heartbroken does not convey the exhaustion, terror and grief since July 13,” said Cron.

Before, Chitam said, “people feared what an encounter with ICE could mean.” Now, they know it means “they may not return home.”

There is a “collectively shared fear that mistaken identity could mean our death,” she added, noting that the week of Guerrero’s death, the hotline was called 128 times by people seeking guidance and support.

And we heard from Guerrero’s parents, who bravely traveled to the U.S. from Colombia, to ensure that their grief and calls for justice would be included in the public record.

Omar Durán Plata and Dora Guerrero described a kind, hardworking, and loving son.

“Our dream was to be reunited and hold each other again,” Durán Plata said through a translator. Durán Plata said they ask only of God and the justice system that his case be brought to light.

And after hearing all that was said, I left feeling deeply that anyone, particularly those who have a semblance of power, who stands in the way of that justice and who does not try to stop these operations is complicit.

text:
A count of those working for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security who have been charged with sex crimes or violence against women and children took a big jump on Tuesday.

The vast majority of the accused worked for Border Patrol or Immigration and Customs Enforcement — the agencies tasked with President Donald Trump’s controversial mass deportations.

The Ohio Immigrant Alliance started searching court records after it was revealed last year that an ICE supervisor in Cincinnati had a lengthy history of violence against a woman with whom he lived. His history included 23 police visits to his house.

A year earlier, a federal jury convicted an ICE deportation officer in Cincinnati of extorting sex from women over whom he held power.

An earlier version of the report listed 59 Homeland Security employees who had been charged or convicted. The newest version lists 152.

Some of the cases stretch back to the 1980s. But Lynn Tramonte, founder of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance, pointed out that criminality appears to be accelerating as Trump rapidly adds agents to his border-enforcement operation.

Just under one-fourth of the charges and convictions Tramonte and her team found happened since the beginning of the second Trump administration. Fifty-six percent of those on the updated list have been sentenced for their offenses.

About 90% of all cases involve allegations of sexual abuse or gender-based violence, Tramonte said, adding that just over half involved sexual abuse of children. In just under 45% of cases, agents were alleged to have abused their official authority as they committed crimes, she said.

Questions about agents’ vetting and training grew intense last winter when ICE agents in Minneapolis shot two U.S. citizens to death under questionable circumstances.

In July another ICE officer, David Brouillette, shot and killed a Columbian man in Maine. His ex-wife and some former friends told NPR that Brouillette had a long history of racism and violence.

In an email, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said it vets new agents adequately and holds them accountable when they commit abuses.

“The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors,” the spokesperson said.

“We take allegations regarding misconduct seriously and cherish the public’s trust. We work tirelessly to uphold the rule of law and hold ourselves accountable.”

Peter L. Markowitz, a professor at Yeshiva University’s Cardozo School of Law, said the list published by the Ohio Immigrant Alliance proves otherwise.

“One of the things that really stood out to me in this report is how plainly it exposed the hypocrisy of the federal immigration authorities,” he said during a virtual press conference. “We’re hearing the claims over and over again from ICE, from the White House about how they’re going after the worst of the worst.

“But we’ve known for a while that the data just doesn’t match the rhetoric. The most recent data is that about 2% of the most recent immigration court filings involve any criminality at all. Meanwhile, this report is documenting that some of the worst of the worst are in fact employed by ICE. I don’t think this is going to come as a huge surprise to the American public because we’re seeing daily the brutality on our social media feeds.”

Markowitz and Tramonte said that an obvious reform would be to acknowledge that the government is seeking to deport less than 2% of the 66,000 people detained by ICE and Border Patrol based on allegations of criminality. In other words, the overwhelming majority are being held under civil and not criminal law.

Markowitz said “cooperative enforcement strategies” should be employed with documented immigrants.

“ICE is a federal agency that enforces civil law, just like the IRS, the” Securities and Exchange Commission and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, he said. “All these other agencies enforce their laws without using handcuffs and putting people behind bars.”

Those agencies can start a process that leads to criminal charges, “but their first instinct is not to initiate punitive enforcement actions to bring the harshest penalty possible. Instead they try to help the regulated entity to come into compliance.”

Markowitz said immigration authorities have pathways to do something similar.

“Unfortunately, ICE is doing exactly the opposite,” he said. “They’re creating enforcement problems instead of solving enforcement problems.”

title: New Mexico U.S. Rep. Leger Fernández denounces ICE arrest in Santa Fe healthcare clinic ...
authors: Patrick Lohmann, Pierrette Hondagneu-Sotelo, Michael Messner
description:

She asked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and CoreCivic, the facility’s private operator, whether she could speak with any of the people ICE detained in the clinic’s parking lot.

As for the visit to the detention facility in Estancia, she said being denied an interview with those detained in Santa Fe capped off a “disappointing” inspection of the facility, she said.

text:
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M) is seeking answers from federal immigration authorities following reports that agents arrested one or more people in the parking lot of a Santa Fe healthcare facility on Wednesday, including the parent of a child who was left alone.

Leger Fernández told Source NM she was preparing for a previously scheduled inspection of the Torrance County Detention Facility on Wednesday when she learned about the federal immigration operation at La Familia Medical Center in Santa Fe. She asked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and CoreCivic, the facility’s private operator, whether she could speak with any of the people ICE detained in the clinic’s parking lot.

“We did make a request,” she said. “They told us that they anticipated there would be eight detainees arriving to the facility, but that they had not yet gotten there when we were there.”

After videos and photographs of the Santa Fe operation gained traction online, La Familia officials on Wednesday posted to social media noting that federal agents were parked in the organization’s Alto Clinic parking lot to make an arrest and that no officers entered the clinic building.

Still, the arrest has prompted widespread outcry from New Mexico elected officials, including Leger Fernández, who told Source NM that ICE should not be “stalking people” to health clinics to make arrests.

“The fact that they are in Santa Fe conducting these raids so that they can meet a quota has nothing to do with getting the ‘worst of the worst,’” she said. “It’s all about meeting a quota.”

ICE spokesperson Leticia Zamarripa referred Source NM’s questions about the arrest to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond Thursday.

New Mexico House Majority Leader Rep. Reena Szczepanski (D-Santa Fe) in a statement Wednesday said she was outraged that ICE agents “followed a parent and child from their home to a neighborhood health clinic, then arrested that parent in the parking lot.”

“This Administration’s cruel acts turn places of safety and care into places of fear. No parent should have to worry that getting medical care for their child will put them at risk of detention. I will do all I can to protect immigrant safety in our community.”

Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland also denounced the parking lot arrest in a post Wednesday evening as “absolutely unacceptable.”

Leger Fernández said members of her staff have spoken to eyewitnesses of the arrest and that she is hoping to find the family of the person or people arrested to continue to find answers.

As for the visit to the detention facility in Estancia, she said being denied an interview with those detained in Santa Fe capped off a “disappointing” inspection of the facility, she said.

ICE and CoreCivic officials intervened to prevent her from speaking to any detainees, she said, and the facility seemed to have been hastily sanitized ahead of her arrival. Torrance is one of three facilities in the state that houses ICE detainees, who have alleged poor water quality and health concerns amid an ongoing water shortage in Estancia.

“You could smell the cleaner as you were walking, right? They had sanitized the place and emptied the hall, so that we were not able to actually see anybody,” she said.

Leger Fernández’s visit marked the first time a member of Congress has inspected the facility since CoreCivic and ICE entered into a direct contract governing the facility without Torrance County’s involvement. The two parties opted to contract directly after the Legislature enacted the Immigrant Safety Act, which prohibited public entities like counties from contracting with ICE for the purposes of immigrant detention.

In a statement Thursday, CoreCivic spokesperson Ryan Gustin told Source NM that ICE, and not CoreCivic, “determines who is permitted to speak with detainees at its facilities,” and referred additional comment to that agency.

“More broadly, our Torrance County Detention Facility (TCDF) operates under federal detention standards with ICE personnel onsite, and the facility is subject to regular audits and inspections by our government partners. The safety and well-being of the people in our care is our top priority,” Gustin said.

title: DHS has not verified its claim of nearly 16,000 noncitizen voters in Nevada - MS NOW
authors: Zack Stanton, Vaughn Hillyard, Laura Barrón-López, Jordan Rubin, Erum Salam
description:
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that the Trump administration found more than 250,000 “potential” noncitizens on voter rolls across four states, including 15,903 unlawfully registered in Nevada.
He threatened to prosecute election officials if they did not hand over sensitive voter data.
In email exchanges just this week, state officials continued to press for names and addresses for registered voters so that they could verify the administration’s claims.
The list shared with Nevada also included 6,218 other individuals with the highest number of matching attributes.
Among the DHS officials on the call was Heather Honey, who identified herself in the meeting as a senior counselor to Mullin.
text:
Senior Department of Homeland Security officials told Nevada election administrators last week that the Trump administration had not verified its claim that nearly 16,000 noncitizens are illegally registered to vote in the state, and had identified only 185 potential noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls, according to emails and a video recording obtained by MS NOW.

The department had yet to review more than 14,000 additional names as of Aug. 20, according to the material, which Nevada’s secretary of state released in response to a public records request.

Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that the Trump administration found more than 250,000 “potential” noncitizens on voter rolls across four states, including 15,903 unlawfully registered in Nevada. He threatened to prosecute election officials if they did not hand over sensitive voter data. The department has since identified 185 potential noncitizens on Nevada’s voter rolls.

“The documents [and] the lists you spoke of — are we able to get those either now or perhaps immediately following the call?” asked Mark A. Wlaschin, Nevada’s deputy secretary of state for elections, regarding the administration’s claimed list of noncitizen voters.

“We’re not finished going through the voter roll for Nevada, so we wouldn’t have a full and complete list,” said Kimberley Vogt, the fraud division chief with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. “We’re going to manually review to be sure that it is not someone’s dad or someone’s son and that it is that person. Then we’re reducing the list down to what is a confirmed match. We intend to send you guys a list of the ones that we’ve confirmed and they do not appear to be a citizen.”

Murphy Hebert, the chief deputy in the Nevada secretary of state’s office, responded, “So what you’re saying is the 15,000 number has not been vetted, basically? It’s the number that you are starting [with].”

“It hasn’t had a full manual review of each one,” Vogt responded, in part. “It’s a lot of work to go one by one, I’m sure you can imagine.”

Paul Gleason, who works in the fraud division of USCIS, told the Nevada officials that the federal government used data from publicly available voter files in the state, and sought to match them with USCIS records to create a list of potential noncitizens.

“Do you have a rough timeline for when we might be able to receive that information? I mean, given the close proximity not only to Election Day itself but to mail ballots [being sent],” Wlaschin asked.

DHS said on the call that its review of voters is ongoing, but it has not shared a full list with the state, making it difficult for the state to verify any of its information. In email exchanges just this week, state officials continued to press for names and addresses for registered voters so that they could verify the administration’s claims.

Recommended

“Weeks after the President held a national, primetime speech making sweeping claims regarding noncitizens and the security of our elections, DHS representatives informed our office that the numbers that were provided to the public are preliminary and that there is not high enough confidence to be able to share the full dataset with Nevada officials,” Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar said in a statement to MS NOW. “The Secretary of State’s Office will not risk disenfranchising eligible voters and ripping away their Constitutional right to vote without the highest confidence of their ineligibility.”

In a statement to MS NOW after this article was published, an unidentified spokesperson for DHS disputed this reporting. “This is false,” said the spokesperson. “The 185 are the individuals that had gone through manual review. The list shared with Nevada also included 6,218 other individuals with the highest number of matching attributes. This was at the request of NV. They wanted to start with a subset less than the 15,903.”

Trump and the White House have claimed — without substantiation — that noncitizen voting could sway the outcome of U.S. elections, and have directed federal agents across DHS to look for noncitizen voter fraud.

Multiple state election administrators told MS NOW that they are concerned the Trump administration will seek to use claims about noncitizen registered voters to interfere with the November elections — potentially seeking to seize ballots or tabulation machines through a search warrant or an attempted declaration of a national emergency by Trump.

Among the DHS officials on the call was Heather Honey, who identified herself in the meeting as a senior counselor to Mullin. In March 2025, Honey suggested the president should declare a “national emergency” ahead of the midterm elections to address claims of fraudulent voting, The New York Times has reported. Months later, Trump appointed her DHS’ deputy assistant secretary for election integrity, a role in which she has steered department resources toward searching for noncitizens on voter rolls or evidence of voter fraud.

Prior to joining the administration, Honey led the Pennsylvania chapter of the Election Integrity Network — an umbrella group for state-level election activists who fought the certification of the 2020 election. That national organization is helmed by Cleta Mitchell, who advised Trump’s effort to overturn the 2020 result and organized a remote White House briefing in July for election conspiracy theorists about declassified election material.

description:

text:
The recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling on June 23, 2026 on the case Lau v. Garland has changed how lawful permanent residents (green card holders) may be treated when returning to the United States after travel abroad. This decision expands the government’s authority to question, detain, and place green card holders into immigration proceedings based on allegations, even without a criminal conviction.

What has changed?

The Supreme Court ruled that immigration officials do not need clear and convincing evidence of wrongdoing before treating a green card holder as if they are seeking admission into the U.S. This means:

You may be treated like a non-resident when re-entering the country.

Officials may rely on allegations, not proven facts.

You could be placed in deportation proceedings more easily.

This is especially concerning when tied to the vague concept of a “crime involving moral turpitude,” which does not have a clear or consistent definition.

Who Is Most at Risk?

While this ruling affects all green card holders, some individuals may face a higher risk:

People with any past arrests, charges, or pending criminal cases (even without conviction).

Individuals who have spent extended time outside of the U.S.

Those with prior immigration issues or past encounters with law enforcement.

Community members from groups historically subject to heightened scrutiny.

Key Risks to Be Aware Of

Being detained or questioned at the airport or border.

Being placed in immigration proceedings without a conviction.

Being pressured to sign documents or give up rights.

Facing uncertainty about re-entry after traveling abroad.

Before traveling :

Consult an immigration attorney if you have any criminal history, no matter how minor or old.

Avoid international travel if you have pending legal issues or unresolved cases.

Carry proof of your ties to the U.S. (Job, family, residence).

When returning to the U.S.

Stay calm and do not panic

Do not sign any documents without speaking to a lawyer.

You have the right to ask for an attorney, though access may be delayed at the border.

Do not provide false information.

Know Your Rights :

You are a Lawful Permanent Resident and have legal status.

You are not required to answer all questions beyond basic information.

You can request to speak with a lawyer before making decisions.

If You Are Detained:

Ask to contact a Lawyer immediately.

Contact a trusted family member or friend.

Do not sign anything you do not understand.

This ruling increases uncertainty and risk, but you are not alone. Community organizations, legal advocates, and immigrant rights groups are actively working to support affected individuals and push for stronger protections.

Remember

Your green card still grants you lawful permanent resident status, but this decision means that additional caution is necessary — especially when traveling. Staying informed and prepared is the best way to protect yourself and your loved ones.

text:
The man accused of operating an illegal charter boat that capsized in New York Harbor, killing a mother and her baby, has been arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, officials said Thursday.

The Department of Homeland Security said an investigation found Manuel Hernandez, who is from El Salvador, has been living in the U.S. illegally.

“Once he faces justice for his crimes, we will make sure that he is swiftly removed from our country,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.

Hernandez, 46, was conducting a paid boat tour near Liberty Island on Aug. 8 when the vessel capsized, killing 27-year-old Sarah Sanchez and her 5-month-old daughter Antonella Garcia, authorities said.

Federal prosecutors said 14 people were on board the boat at the time — four more than its 10-person maximum.

The vessel had no infant life vests onboard, but Hernandez let the 5-month-old ride anyway, telling her parents one of them could wear their own life jacket and hold her, according to a federal complaint.

He was charged with two counts of misconduct and neglect of a ship officer resulting in death earlier this month.

text:
(NewsNation) — After months of anxious anticipation, Haitian refugees previously protected from deportation while living in Ohio are facing expedited deportation after being arrested by federal immigration officers who are now surging in communities with large Haitian populations.

Springfield, which boasts between 10,000 and 15,000 Haitian refugees as residents and local business owners, has witnessed an uptick in arrests of refugees over the past week. A growing number of inmates at the Butler County Jail are designated as “Hold for ICE” as the Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration across the country continues.

The presence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in the community intensified in ways residents had not experienced before. Local advocates told NewsNation that ICE officers are now detaining Haitians at their homes and that a Haitian pastor was taken into custody at a local gas station.

ICE officers were recently given guidance indicating that former “Temporary Protected Status” holders should “first be considered for expedited removal,” The New York Times reported recently.

TPS for Haitians ended July 27 after a Supreme Court ruling cleared the way for the administration to move ahead with terminating previous protections for 350,000 Haitians living in the United States.

Over the past week, ICE officers have increased their presence in Springfield. Marjorie Wentworth, a Springfield resident who serves on the board of directors for the Haitian Community Help & Support Center, said many of the arrests that have taken place this week are occurring as Haitians are arriving at their jobs or on their way home from work.

Vilès Dorsainvil, the support center’s executive director, who came to Ohio in 2020 from Haiti, has referred to the current environment in Springfield as “extremely chaotic.” The uptick in federal immigration officers comes two years after JD Vance, the former Republican U.S. senator from Ohio and Donald Trump’s running mate, alleged Haitian refugees were stealing their neighbors’ pets and eating them.

Vance posted on X, without evidence, that Springfield has experienced “a massive rise in communicable diseases, rent prices, car insurance rates, and crime.”

Springfield Mayor Rob Rue said in a statement issued Wednesday that city officials had been notified that officers from ICE’s enforcement and removals operations division are conducting operations in Springfield and in surrounding areas. City officials were also told that targeted enforcement activity will continue throughout Ohio.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson declined to address the guidance reportedly given to ICE officers when asked for comment by NewsNation. Instead, the spokesperson said Wednesday that DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe.

“For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent,” the spokesperson said, adding, “What we would say now is (that) it’s closing time, which means you don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here.”

Haitian refugees forced to wear ankle monitors, limiting travel

In addition to the recent arrests, more than 100 others have been summoned since July to ICE offices outside Cincinnati, more than an hour away, local officials said.

Haitian refugees began receiving summonses in the mail in July to appear at immigration hearings, after which they were fitted and issued ankle bracelets.

For Dorsainvil, the monitors were the latest way that the Trump administration was looking to intimidate Haitian refugees. Once there, refugees are forced to surrender their passports to ICE officials and return to Springfield wearing the ankle monitors, which allow federal immigration officers to track their movements.

Additionally, Haitians forced to wear the monitors are not permitted to travel more than 75 miles from their homes, according to multiple media reports.

Dorsainvil said that the electronic monitoring of Haitians that is now leading to arrests taking place in Springfield is the latest way the Trump administration is terrorizing refugees.

“It is so humiliating to see parents, fathers and mothers, who have not been committing any crime now, with some type of ankle bracelets on their feet,” Dorsainvil told NewsNation local affiliate WCMH. “That has created so much fear.”

Wentworth told NewsNation that there is a marked difference in how ICE is conducting its enforcement operations compared to other cities like Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis.

Yet despite the lack of previous public-facing enforcement tactics that included the use of tear gas and other nonlethal munitions, the presence of ICE officers and unmarked federal vehicles that have been seen patrolling Springfield streets over the past week has sparked fear among those being targeted.

“You can just feel that it’s different,” Wentworth said this week. “But if you’re from Haiti, it doesn’t feel different.”

“People are terrified,” she added. “It was already bad enough (before). But now, these people are being traumatized … and they’re being forced to make horrible decisions.”

Although previous threats of ICE activity created a sense of anxiety for Haitians, refugees are not leaving their homes and going about their normal daily activities over the past week, Wentworth said. A local church where the congregation is made up almost entirely of Haitians canceled its services last weekend as reports of increased ICE presence began to make its way around town.

Haitian green-card holders who have opened and run businesses in Springfield are no longer showing up for work, Wentworth said amid the increased ICE activity that had been forecasted for months.

Thursday’s arrest of the local Haitian pastor has also spiked anxiety levels both among Haitians and those working around the clock to provide humanitarian services like food delivery to more than 10,000 residents who have become engrained in the community’s fabric.

“We recognize that this activity may create concern and uncertainty for members of our community,” Rue said in a statement released by his office Wednesday. “We ask everyone to continue to treat everyone with dignity and respect and allow our public safety personnel to continue their work of keeping Springfield safe.”

title: Border Cops Detained Me for Hours Without Explanation. They Won't Tell Me Why. - Yahoo
description:
The Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agent at the front desk refused.
After stamping my wife's passport around 6:30 a.m., the CBP agent at passport control told me that I had to go "somewhere else."
But at the secondary screening desk, a CBP agent told her that she wouldn't be walking to that appointment as a free woman.
My lawyer told me to hang tight, because as an American, they have to let me in eventually.
Last year, CBP detained lawyer Amir Makled and demanded to search his phone, which he was partially successful at refusing.
text:
Around the fourth hour of my detention at the airport, I decided to ask for a lawyer. The Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agent at the front desk refused. I told him that he can't indefinitely hold an American citizen. "It's not indefinite," he replied. "We'll let you know."

That little exchange captures the absolute power that CBP claims over travelers, including Americans, going far beyond any domestic law enforcement interrogation. You don't have a right to contact a lawyer. Neither do you have a right to know why you're being detained or what will happen next. It's not "indefinite" detention; they just won't tell you what the "definite" part is. Crossing the U.S. border is the closest most Americans will come to experiencing life under the foreign dictatorships I report on.

I am not the only American journalist or researcher to be held up at the border. Nor was my experience particularly bad. I got out in four hours with all of my possessions intact. But I decided to do something that most others don't: I reached out to CBP and asked why they did what they did to me. And I asked them about an earlier interrogation, during the Biden administration, which in hindsight seemed inappropriate.

At first, CBP's media office was quite helpful. The first spokesperson I spoke to promised to pull up the notes from my two interrogations, and pointed me to the hotline for travelers who have had excessive "difficulties during travel screening." As days turned to a week and I was passed between different CBP staff, it became clear that I wasn't getting a straight answer. One spokesperson apologized for being "distracted" with more urgent stories. Another was on leave for several days. Et cetera.

It was clear that CBP had the information. One of the spokespeople actually corrected me on the date of my first interrogation—May 16, 2023—so they clearly had looked over my file. But I wasn't getting anything other than generic, anonymous answers: "CBP officers have the authority to ask a wide range of questions, including about travel locations and contacts there. Officers may also ask questions out of curiosity about travel location or your work in media."

The first time I wound up in an interrogation room was in May 2023, flying into John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York from a Fulbright study abroad in Jordan. As I wrote at the time, the process was quick and professional. But in hindsight, parts of it were disturbing. The agents wanted to know if I "have any family in any of those countries" that I was traveling in. When I mentioned that my Fulbright project involved helping Jordanian journalists with translation, they asked, "What kind of media?"

One of the beautiful things about America is that neither my journalism nor my ethnic background are the government's business, except, apparently, at the border.

I reentered the country without incident every time after that, until last week. After spending the beginning of this year abroad—studying, getting married to a foreigner, setting up our new home, and hanging out with my in-laws—my wife and I wanted to visit my family in New Jersey. Worried that my wife would become one of the many tourists on valid visas turned away, we contacted a lawyer and wrote down his number before traveling.

To our surprise, I was the one who had trouble getting into my own country. After stamping my wife's passport around 6:30 a.m., the CBP agent at passport control told me that I had to go "somewhere else." That meant secondary inspection. I was handed my passport in a locked plastic box with a bright orange lid and pointed toward a seemingly endless corridor. I told my wife to contact the lawyer if it took "too long."

The waiting room at the end of the corridor was a strange mix of professional courtesy and casual cruelty. I saw agents ask a young man what kind of food they should bring him and reassure an old man that everything will be sorted out. I also saw agents snap at someone who wanted to use the bathroom. "Did you think you could just do that without asking?" an agent shouted as the man walked toward the bathroom door.

An older Jordanian woman was there with her American husband. She had gotten an email informing her of a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services appointment, so she boarded the next plane from Amman to Washington that she could find. But at the secondary screening desk, a CBP agent told her that she wouldn't be walking to that appointment as a free woman. He was taking away the woman's green card for being outside America for too long. She could either sign away the green card on the spot, or be detained and taken to a judge.

As the woman broke down in tears and her husband frantically tried to contact a lawyer, the agent went back to laughing with his colleagues about football.

Wary of the stories I've covered about CBP searching electronics, I didn't bring a working cellphone with me. Around 10:10 a.m., I walked up to the intake desk for the waiting room and asked to use their landline phone. "Our landline?" the agent replied, confused that I would even ask. I said that I wanted to contact a lawyer. He flat-out refused.

"Since the international arrivals inspection is an administrative function, CBP policy and federal regs do not permit the presence of lawyers during secondary examinations," CBP spokesman Stephen Sapp tells me. In other words, when I'm under an administrative rather than a criminal investigation, I have fewer rights than someone accused of a crime.

Sitting back down in the waiting room, I saw another American waiting with his foreign wife, and asked to use his phone to text my lawyer. My lawyer told me to hang tight, because as an American, they have to let me in eventually. (Unfortunately, there is no legal limit to how long "eventually" can be.) He was also busy reassuring my wife, who was sitting in baggage claims asking herself, Where can they possibly deport my husband? New Jersey?

Finally, at around 10:30 a.m., an agent at a secondary screening desk called my name. He asked me a few basic questions about my itinerary for the past year. Although it would have been my right to refuse even those questions—all I have to demonstrate to CBP is that I'm an American citizen—I saw no harm in telling him information that the government already has. The agent was quite polite, apologetic about the wait, and offered to help me find my wife in the arrivals hall after clearing me for entry. He also offered no answers about why I was being held up in the first place.

"They let my wife through but took me. I don't know why," I told the agent in response to his question about who I traveled with. "I don't know why either," he responded, facepalming.

When I later texted the same information to a source who used to work in immigration, he responded, "????" He speculates that I'm either "on a list but a vague one," or my itinerary triggered some kind of automatic alert. As Reason has covered, automated border control systems often take away the personal discretion that officials have, and even deprive them of knowing the reasons behind decisions the computer is making. And the government is moving toward AI-generated watch lists.

In theory, CBP has no right to stop Americans from coming home. There is no condition for a U.S. citizen to enter the U.S. other than proving their citizenship. CBP does have authority to search anyone, citizens or otherwise, for contraband goods at the border. (Controversially, the agency claims that right extends to electronic data.) So-called "secondary screening" is often an opportunity to squeeze information out of Americans, especially because exhausted travelers might not know or assert their rights.

Last year, CBP detained lawyer Amir Makled and demanded to search his phone, which he was partially successful at refusing. A few months later, immigration attorney Andrew Lattarulo sued CBP for seizing his phone, claiming that it was retaliation for criticizing the Trump administration. A judge ruled that the feds can't look at the data on it. Last month, CBP demanded that Vermont school superintendent Wilmer Chavarria give up the passwords to his work phone and work laptop, claiming that it would "stain" his record to refuse, according to Chavarria.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) acknowledges maintaining a variety of databases and watch lists on travelers, including the Automated Targeting System and the Secure Flight lists. And then there are the lists that the government doesn't even acknowledge exist. During the first Trump administration, CBP compiled a secret list of journalists and lawyers to question at the border. Earlier this year, an immigration lawyer accidentally discovered a document titled "watch list" on a DHS website, which appears to be a list of immigration lawyers.

Of course, travelers don't have any way of knowing they're on any of these lists until they run into problems. That's part of the arbitrary power CBP and other Homeland Security agencies exercise: You, the humble citizen, have no way to predict or prepare for how you'll be treated.

For all the dictatorial powers that CBP and its Skynet-like systems have at the border, America is still a democracy domestically. I let CBP's press office know that I was going to exercise my First Amendment rights to write about my two experiences in secondary screening, and the spokesman seemed quite eager to get me information, a tone I previously hadn't experienced from CBP spokespeople.

The same source who explained my potential watch-listing told me that "no DHS person wants to be noticed…especially if they have pulled in the 'wrong' kind of person." Unlike many of the other reporters and academics detained at the border, I've written a lot for publications on the political right, including ones that are close to the Trump administration's base.

But Americans shouldn't have to be a specific kind of journalist to get answers about why the government is hassling them. (Frankly, neither should foreign guests who are following the rules.) Going home after a long trip is not a crime. And however much CBP insists that secondary inspection is an "administrative function," not a criminal investigation, that's a distinction without a difference for someone who's being asked intrusive questions and can't leave.

Fortunately, there's a route that's open to everyone. I have filed a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request for all the data that CBP has on me, from agents' field notes to any automated system hits. However long it takes for CBP to respond, and however heavily they redact the documents, I'm legally entitled to a response. And so are you.

title: RAC-MA Campaign Update: The PROTECT Act Passes! - Religious Action Center
description:
On August 6, Governor Maura Healey signed the PROTECT Act.
The passage of the PROTECT Act serves as the culmination of our efforts at RAC-MA over the past year to protect the civil rights of immigrants in the state.
The act provides a variety of other safeguards such as translated notices of rights, rights to confidential communications with attorneys, etc.
The law limits law enforcement cooperation with ICE including through 287(g) agreements that permit law enforcement to assist ICE with apprehension and detention.
Immigration justice legislation previously backed by RAC-MA - the "Dignity not Deportations" Act - did not advance successfully from committee.
text:
We are pleased to share some good news with our Religious Action Center - Massachusetts (RAC-MA) supporters. On August 6, Governor Maura Healey signed the PROTECT Act. The PROTECT Act is Massachusetts' first comprehensive piece of legislation to, as stated in its full title, advance "rule of law, oversight, trust, and equal constitutional treatment" of our immigrant neighbors. The passage of the PROTECT Act serves as the culmination of our efforts at RAC-MA over the past year to protect the civil rights of immigrants in the state.

As Reform Jews, support for the rule of law and the civil rights of vulnerable populations advances our goal of Tikkun Olam - our aspiration to repair the world and extend justice to all of our fellow human beings - and fulfills our duty, as we are instructed 36 times in the Torah, to protect the stranger or sojourner. We are proud to stand together with other Reform Jews to take a step toward achieving this sacred goal.

Throughout this campaign, we worked with a broad coalition of immigration rights, civil rights and faith-based justice organizations in the People's Protect Act coalition, writing letters, submitting testimony, and organizing actions including two "Lobby Day" events at the State House and a coordinated "call-in" campaign directed at key legislators working on the bill. Among its many provisions, the bill includes the following safeguards:

Due process protections for immigrant detainees. The PROTECT Act bans warrantless civil immigration arrests in sensitive locations including schools and health care facilities and, perhaps most importantly, courthouses and courthouse grounds. The act provides a variety of other safeguards such as translated notices of rights, rights to confidential communications with attorneys, etc.

Limits on state and local law enforcement collaboration with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The law limits law enforcement cooperation with ICE including through 287(g) agreements that permit law enforcement to assist ICE with apprehension and detention.

Expedited approval of "U & T" visas. These visas provide a pathway to legal status for survivors of human trafficking and violent crimes who assist with criminal investigations. Among other provisions, this section of the law reduces the wait time for such visas from 90 to 45 days.

Initially, it was not at all clear that our efforts would be successful. In September, House Speaker Mariano was publicly skeptical that immigration justice legislation would pass during the current session, hedging that he did not "know whether it was the year" to pass legislation protecting immigrant rights. Immigration justice legislation previously backed by RAC-MA - the "Dignity not Deportations" Act - did not advance successfully from committee. However, backed by the sustained support of RAC-MA and many other partners, the Black and Latino Caucus of the state legislature advanced the first version of the PROTECT Act, combining elements of the Dignity Not Deportations Act with pieces of other legislation being considered, such as the Safe Communities Act, ultimately resulting in the signed bill.

The PROTECT Act is not perfect. We and other members of our coalition had hoped for a stronger version of the limitation on 287(g) ICE-law enforcement collaboration agreements, closer to if not completely banning this practice of using our local and state resources in abusive immigration enforcement practices. The law allows authorities to appeal to the governor and attorney general for time-limited agreements approved for a legitimate law enforcement purpose. It is the position of the RAC that immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility, and we should rely on local and state law enforcement for carrying out law enforcement duties. We are also deeply opposed to ICE's repeated assaults on the rights of immigrants and peaceful protestors.

This coming year, RAC-MA will transition to a new legislative campaign. The campaign may be immigration justice-related or focus on one of the many other social and economic justice areas that demand our attention as Reform Jews. We will continue to stand with our partners in the People's Protect Act Coalition to further advance the cause of immigration justice at the local and state level, just as the national RAC will continue pursuing reforms that can only be addressed at the federal level.

Join us on Wednesday, September 9th at 6pm for a celebration of the hard work of all of the RAC-MA advocates who were a part of this crucial effort to treat our fellow human beings justly and compassionately. We look forward to congratulating all of you on a job well done, though there is more left to do. As Pirkei Avot teaches us, it is not our duty to finish the work, but we must engage in it. Thank you for helping us achieve this important beginning.

text:
Days after federal immigration officers attempted to search a Sacramento law firm, the Sacramento City Council member representing that district is calling the incident a "flagrant abuse of power" that "must never be tolerated."

Lisa Kaplan represents District 1, where the Morris Law Group is located. The firm assists clients with obtaining citizenship, including asylum seekers and crime victims who are legally allowed to use the firm's address as a safe mailing address.

Attorney Raissa Morris, head of the firm, believes the nature of her practice is what made her business a target. While she herself was not present at the time, her employees recalled the interaction to her.

The employees told her that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived in unmarked cars, some without license plates, and with dark-tinted windows. They were also armed.

Morris' staff told the agents that they could not come through without a warrant, but Morris said one of the agents threatened to return if the firm did not comply.

"The attempt by ICE to target an immigration law firm with an illegal search in District 1 is a flagrant abuse of power meant purely for harassment and intimidation and a direct assault on the rule of law," Kaplan said in a statement in response. "They are not battlegrounds for political intimidation. Weaponizing federal agencies to bully advocates and scare vulnerable communities undermines justice for everyone. We must demand immediate accountability and fiercely protect the integrity of our legal systems and constitutional rights."

This incident has also drawn the attention of California U.S. Sen. Adam Schiff, who said in a social media post that he plans to launch an investigation. He called the agents' conduct "unconscionable."

"ICE should know they cannot enter private property without a judicial warrant," Schiff said. "Instead of complying with the law, ICE agents chose to threaten violence against a law firm because of whom they represent."

Morris stated that if ICE agents return, they will need a search warrant signed by a judge.

In a statement to KCRA 3, DHS said, “On August 14, ICE officers approached an unmarked door during a targeted enforcement operation, thinking it was the target address as it was listed as the address of the illegal aliens they were planning to arrest. Upon finding out it was a law firm; they departed the address.”

text:
Federal

Trump Signs New Executive Orders Targeting Birthright Citizenship After Supreme Court Loss

President Trump signed two executive orders on August 6 seeking to narrow birthright citizenship, five weeks after the Supreme Court ruled June 30 in Trump v. Barbara that his earlier attempt to deny citizenship based on parents’ immigration status violated the Fourteenth Amendment. The first order, “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship,” denies citizenship to children born in the U.S. when neither parent is a citizen and one parent is a foreign government employee, an “alien enemy” tied to a designated terrorist group, someone who obtained a U.S. birth through a commercial surrogacy or fraud-related transaction, or a resident of a territory where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute. The second order, “Ending Birth Tourism,” directs the State Department and Department of Homeland Security to deny or revoke visas, block entry, and pursue enforcement against foreign nationals and facilitators who travel to the U.S. specifically to give birth.

The administration argues the orders operate within the narrow historical exceptions to birthright citizenship that the Supreme Court affirmed in June, such as the long-recognized exclusion for children of accredited diplomats, rather than reviving the broader approach the Court struck down. Civil rights groups reject that framing, and several advocacy organizations sued the administration on August 11. They asked a federal judge to block enforcement of the new orders, arguing they represent another unconstitutional attempt to undermine a citizenship guarantee the Supreme Court has already upheld. Courts will now have to decide whether the administration is applying exceptions the Supreme Court already recognized or manufacturing new ones the Court has already rejected, leaving families, agencies, and officials who document citizenship facing renewed uncertainty until that question is resolved.

DHS Proposes Ending 60-Day Grace Period for H-1B Visa Holders and Imposes Biometric Fee

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) submitted a proposed rule to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) on August 6 that would eliminate the 60-day grace period currently afforded to H-1B, L-1, E, TN, and other nonimmigrant visa holders whose employment ends before their authorized stay expires. Under current rules, workers who lose their jobs can remain in the U.S. for up to 60 days to find new employment or change status. If the grace period is eliminated, affected workers and their dependents would generally have to leave the country immediately and would be unable to change status or employers unless U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) grants discretionary relief. The rule has not yet been published in the Federal Register and will be subject to a 30- to 60-day public comment period once it clears OMB review, meaning the existing grace period remains in effect for now.

Separately, DHS finalized a rule, published August 10 and taking effect September 9, that expands the $4,000 “9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee” for H-1B petitions (and $4,500 for L-1 petitions) to cover all extension-of-status filings, not just initial petitions or change-of-employer requests. The fee applies to employers with at least 50 U.S. employees where more than half the workforce holds H-1B or L-1 status, and DHS estimates it will generate an additional $37.9 million in fiscal year 2026 and $40 million in fiscal year 2027. Immigration attorneys note the expanded fee is separate from the $100,000 H-1B entry fee imposed last year, which does not apply to extension petitions, but warn that combined with the potential loss of the grace period, employers and workers could face significantly higher costs and less flexibility when navigating job transitions.

Legal

New Ruling BIA Could Bar Some Advance Parole Holders From Reentering the U.S.

The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) ruled on August 13 in Matter of Delcarmen-Lara that traveling abroad on advance parole can trigger the three- or ten-year unlawful presence bar to reentry, overturning 14 years of precedent set by Matter of Arrabally and Yerrabelly in 2012. Under the prior rule, a trip abroad on advance parole was not considered a “departure” for purposes of the unlawful presence bars, allowing immigrants, including many Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients, who had accrued more than 180 days of unlawful presence to travel and return without jeopardizing a future path to a green card. The BIA rejected that reasoning, concluding that the plain statutory language does not exempt advance parole travel from the ordinary meaning of “departure.” As a result, a person who accrued more than 180 days but less than a year of unlawful presence before departing could now face a three-year bar upon return, while a year or more could trigger a ten-year bar.

The ruling applies only prospectively, so trips taken on advance parole before August 13 are not affected, but the Board explicitly overruled the legal foundation many immigrants and attorneys had relied on for over a decade when advising clients that such travel was safe. Immigrant advocacy groups condemned the decision, warning it could strip DACA recipients and others of a pathway to permanent status simply for having lawfully traveled with government-issued travel authorization.

Judge Steps Up Scrutiny of Children’s Detention Amid Challenges to Flores Rules

A federal judge in Los Angeles ordered new independent oversight of immigrant children’s detention this week, appointing both an independent monitor and a special master after finding that officials at facilities in Texas and California likely held children and other detainees in unsafe temperatures and denied them soap and adequate sleeping conditions. Judge Dolly Gee’s order, issued August 17, comes as she continues to oversee government compliance with the 1997 Flores settlement, the consent decree that sets minimum standards of care for immigrant children in federal custody and generally requires their prompt release.

The ruling lands amid an escalating legal fight over the settlement’s future. The Trump administration has pursued a two-track strategy: pressing the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit to terminate the agreement entirely while simultaneously urging the district court not to impose the kind of independent monitoring Gee has now ordered. The dispute has taken on new urgency amid the administration’s broader expansion of family detention, which has included reopening detention centers in Karnes and Dilley, Texas that had been shuttered since 2021, and reports that hundreds of children have been held well beyond the settlement’s 20-day limit. Judge Gee said during a June hearing that her “patience has come to an end” after years of what she called bad-faith noncompliance, and the Justice Department has simultaneously pressed the 9th Circuit to let the administration scrap the settlement altogether, arguing DHS’s conduct should be judged against current law rather than “a 30-year-old settlement agreement” . Legal experts say that if the 9th Circuit sides with the government, the fight is likely headed to the Supreme Court, meaning Gee’s newly appointed independent monitor could end up enforcing a settlement whose legal survival remains very much in doubt.

University Groups Sue to Block Rule Ending Duration of Status for International Students

A coalition of higher education associations, labor unions, and media groups sued the Department of Homeland Security on August 18, seeking to block a final rule that would replace the decades-old “duration of status” framework for F, J, and I visa holders with fixed admission periods before it takes effect September 15. The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, argues DHS violated the Administrative Procedure Act by failing to adequately assess the rule’s costs and benefits, respond meaningfully to public comments, consider less burdensome alternatives, or justify the regulation based on its stated goals. Plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate the rule entirely and issue a preliminary injunction preventing it from taking effect. Under the rule, F-1 and J-1 students would be capped at four-year admission periods regardless of how long their academic program actually takes, while I visas for foreign journalists would be cut from as long as five years to 240 days, or just 90 days for Chinese nationals; anyone needing more time would have to file a formal extension request with USCIS, including fees and biometric collection. The plaintiffs argue in their complaint that the changes would be “catastrophic” for universities, international students, and scholars, warning that the compressed timeline before the rule’s effective date has left institutions and prospective students with little ability to prepare.

The lawsuit does not automatically pause the rule, meaning it remains scheduled to take effect September 15 unless the court grants a stay beforehand. The case adds to a broader legal and policy fight over the rule, including its effects on Optional Practical Training and the roughly 1.6 million F-1 and 500,000 J-1 visa holders active annually who would be affected by the shift away from duration of status

LEGISLATIVE FLOOR CALENDAR

The U.S. House will return from recess on August 31, and the U.S. Senate will return on September 14.
